chapters.chapter_title: Introduction

chapters_covered: I — Introduction
key_themes: Short title and territorial extent of the Code (Section 1)
Territorial jurisdiction — offences within India (Section 2)
Offences beyond India triable in India under Indian law (Section 3)
Extra-territorial jurisdiction over citizens, Indian ships/aircraft and cyber-offences targeting Indian computer resources (Section 4)
Saving of military laws and special/local laws (Section 5)
notable_amendments: Section 1 — words 'except the State of Jammu and Kashmir' omitted by Act 34 of 2019 (w.e.f. 31-10-2019).
Section 4 — clause (3) (offences targeting a computer resource located in India) inserted by Act 10 of 2009, s. 51 (w.e.f. 27-10-2009).
'British India' successively replaced by 'India' through the A.O. 1948, A.O. 1950 and Act 3 of 1951.
metadata.case_query: An Indian citizen residing abroad hacks into a government server located in Delhi from a foreign country; he argues that Indian courts have no jurisdiction because all his acts were committed outside India.

sections.heading: Preamble
sections.text: WHEREAS it is expedient to provide a general Penal Code for India; It is enacted as follows:—
sections.key_principle: Preamble stating the legislative purpose — a single, general penal code for the whole country. Not an operative provision; it creates no offence.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. successively by the A.O. 1937, A.O. 1948, A.O. 1950 and Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch., for 'British India'.

sections.heading: Title and extent of operation of the Code
sections.text: This Act shall be called the Indian Penal Code, and shall extend to the whole of India.
ingredients: Short title: the Indian Penal Code
Territorial extent: the whole of India
sections.key_principle: Names the Code and fixes its territorial extent. The words 'except the State of Jammu and Kashmir' were omitted by Act 34 of 2019 (w.e.f. 31-10-2019), so the Code now extends to the whole of India.
sections.amendment_note: The words 'except the State of Jammu and Kashmir' omitted by Act 34 of 2019, s. 95 and the Fifth Schedule (w.e.f. 31-10-2019).

footnotes.note_text: The Indian Penal Code has been extended to Berar by the Berar Laws Act, 1941 (4 of 1941) and declared in force in Sonthal Parganas, Panth Piploda, Khondmals District and Angul District by the respective Regulations; declared in force in certain Scheduled Districts under s. 3(a) of the Scheduled Districts Act, 1874; extended to the Lushai Hills under s. 5 of the same Act; and extended to Goa, Daman and Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Pondicherry and Lakshadweep by Regulations of 1962–1965.
The original words have successively been amended by Act 12 of 1891, the A.O. 1937, A.O. 1948 and A.O. 1950 to read as above.
The words 'except the State of Jammu and Kashmir' omitted by Act 34 of 2019, s. 95 and the Fifth Schedule (w.e.f. 31-10-2019).

sections.heading: Punishment of offences committed within India
sections.text: Every person shall be liable to punishment under this Code and not otherwise for every act or omission contrary to the provisions thereof, of which he shall be guilty within India.
ingredients: Any person (no distinction of nationality)
Act or omission contrary to the Code
Committed within India
sections.key_principle: Territorial jurisdiction and the principle of legality: liability arises only under this Code (or other law), 'and not otherwise'. The words 'on or after the said first day of May, 1861' were repealed by Act 12 of 1891.

footnotes.note_text: The original words 'the said territories' successively amended by the A.O. 1937, A.O. 1948, A.O. 1950 and Act 3 of 1951 to read as above.
The words and figures 'on or after the said first day of May, 1861' rep. by Act 12 of 1891, s. 2 and the First Sch.

sections.heading: Punishment of offences committed beyond, but which by law may be tried within, India
sections.text: Any person liable, by any Indian law, to be tried for an offence committed beyond India shall be dealt with according to the provisions of this Code for any act committed beyond India in the same manner as if such act had been committed within India.
ingredients: Person liable under an Indian law to be tried for an offence committed beyond India
Act committed outside India
Dealt with under this Code as if committed within India
sections.key_principle: Extra-territorial offences that Indian law makes triable in India are punished under this Code as if committed within India. Section 3 deals with trial under Indian law; section 4 extends the Code itself to specified extra-territorial offences.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by the A.O. 1937, for 'law passed by the Governor General of India in Council'.
The original words 'the limits of the said territories' successively amended to read as above.

sections.heading: Extension of Code to extra-territorial offences
sections.text: The provisions of this Code apply also to any offence committed by— (1) any citizen of India in any place without and beyond India; (2) any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India wherever it may be; (3) any person in any place without and beyond India committing offence targeting a computer resource located in India.
sections.inserted_by: Clause (3) and the revised Explanation inserted by Act 10 of 2009, s. 51 (w.e.f. 27-10-2009); section substituted by Act 4 of 1898, s. 2; clauses (1)–(2) substituted by the A.O. 1950.
ingredients: Offence committed by an Indian citizen anywhere outside India; OR
Offence committed by any person on an Indian-registered ship or aircraft, wherever it may be; OR
Offence committed by any person outside India targeting a computer resource located in India
sections.key_principle: Three-limbed extra-territorial jurisdiction: nationality (citizens), registration (Indian ships/aircraft) and the cyber-effects limb (clause 3, inserted by Act 10 of 2009). 'Offence' includes any act outside India that would be punishable if committed in India.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, who is a citizen of India, commits a murder in Uganda. He can be tried and convicted of murder in any place in India in which he may be found.
illustrations.verdict: A can be tried in India for murder committed abroad
illustrations.key_principle: An Indian citizen remains subject to the Code for offences committed abroad; trial may be held wherever he is found in India.

explanations.label: Explanation (a)
explanations.text: The word 'offence' includes every act committed outside India which, if committed in India, would be punishable under this Code.
explanations.plain_language: 'Offence' here covers acts done abroad that would have been crimes if done in India.

explanations.label: Explanation (b)
explanations.text: The expression 'computer resource' shall have the meaning assigned to it in clause (k) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2000).
explanations.plain_language: 'Computer resource' takes its meaning from the IT Act, 2000.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 4 of 1898, s. 2, for section 4.
Subs. by the A.O. 1950, for cls. (1) to (4).
Subs. by s. 51, ibid., for the Explanation (w.e.f. 27-10-2009).

sections.heading: Certain laws not to be affected by this Act
sections.text: Nothing in this Act shall affect the provisions of any Act for punishing mutiny and desertion of officers, soldiers, sailors or airmen in the service of the Government of India or the provisions of any special or local law.
ingredients: Acts punishing mutiny and desertion of officers, soldiers, sailors or airmen are saved
Special or local laws are saved
sections.key_principle: Saving clause: the Code does not override the military discipline Acts or any special or local law.

footnotes.note_text: Subs., ibid., for section 5 (A.O. 1950).

chapters.chapter_title: General Explanations

chapters_covered: II — General Explanations
key_themes: Interpretive rules: General Exceptions apply to all offences (s. 6), uniform meaning (s. 7), gender, number, 'man', 'woman', 'person', 'public' (ss. 8–12)
Government-related definitions: 'Government', 'India', 'Judge', 'Court of Justice', 'public servant' (ss. 14–21)
Property and mens rea terms: movable property, wrongful gain/loss, dishonestly, fraudulently, reason to believe (ss. 22–26)
Counterfeit, document, electronic record, valuable security, will (ss. 28–31)
Acts and omissions; joint liability — common intention (s. 34), criminal knowledge/intention (s. 35), co-operation (s. 37), different offences (s. 38)
Voluntarily (s. 39), offence (s. 40), special and local law (ss. 41–42), illegal (s. 43), injury (s. 44)
Life, death, animal, vessel, year/month, section, oath, good faith (ss. 45–52)
notable_amendments: Sections 13, 15, 16 omitted/repealed by the Adaptation Orders of 1937 and 1950.
Section 21 — clause Twelfth substituted by Act 40 of 1964; clause Eleventh inserted by Act 39 of 1920; Rajasthan State amendment adds clause Thirteenth (Rajasthan Act 4 of 1993).
Section 29A (electronic record) inserted by Act 21 of 2000 (w.e.f. 17-10-2000).
Section 34 substituted by Act 27 of 1870 (common intention).
Section 40 substituted by Act 27 of 1870; ss. 118–120 inserted in the extended list by Act 10 of 2009.
metadata.case_query: Three men plan to rob a shopkeeper; during the robbery one of them, without the others' prior knowledge, stabs and kills the shopkeeper. The others argue that they never intended any killing and should not be liable for the death.

sections.heading: Definitions in the Code to be understood subject to exceptions
sections.text: Throughout this Code every definition of an offence, every penal provision, and every illustration of every such definition or penal provision, shall be understood subject to the exceptions contained in the Chapter entitled "General Exceptions", though those exceptions are not repeated in such definition, penal provision, or illustration.
ingredients: Every definition of an offence
Every penal provision
Every illustration
All read subject to Chapter IV (General Exceptions), even if not repeated
sections.key_principle: Rule of construction: the General Exceptions (Chapter IV) are implied into every offence and illustration without being restated.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: The sections, in this Code, which contain definitions of offences, do not express that a child under seven years of age cannot commit such offences; but the definitions are to be understood subject to the general exception which provides that nothing shall be an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.
illustrations.key_principle: Definitions of offences are impliedly subject to the General Exceptions (here, the immunity of a child under seven).

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A, a police-officer, without warrant, apprehends Z, who has committed murder. Here A is not guilty of the offence of wrongful confinement; for he was bound by law to apprehend Z, and therefore the case falls within the general exception which provides that "nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is bound by law to do it".
illustrations.verdict: A not guilty of wrongful confinement
illustrations.key_principle: Acts done in discharge of a legal duty fall within the General Exceptions even though the offence-definition does not mention them.

sections.heading: Sense of expression once explained
sections.text: Every expression which is explained in any part of this Code, is used in every part of this Code in conformity with the explanation.
ingredients: Expression explained anywhere in the Code
Carries the same meaning throughout the Code
sections.key_principle: Uniform-meaning rule: a defined expression has the same sense wherever it appears in the Code, unless the context clearly requires otherwise.

sections.heading: Gender
sections.text: The pronoun "he" and its derivatives are used of any person, whether male or female.
ingredients: Pronoun 'he' and its derivatives
Applies to any person, male or female
sections.key_principle: Gender-neutral reading: 'he' includes women. (The Code later treats certain offences, e.g. outraging modesty, as specific to women where the section so states.)

sections.heading: Number
sections.text: Unless the contrary appears from the context, words importing the singular number include the plural number, and words importing the plural number include the singular number.
ingredients: Singular includes plural
Plural includes singular
Unless context shows the contrary
sections.key_principle: Number rule of construction; context may displace it (e.g. offences requiring a minimum number of persons).

sections.heading: "Man". "Woman".
sections.text: The word "man" denotes a male human being of any age; the word "woman" denotes a female human being of any age.
ingredients: 'Man' = male human being of any age
'Woman' = female human being of any age
sections.key_principle: Age-neutral definitions: a male or female child is a 'man' or 'woman' for the purposes of the Code, though age may matter separately under particular sections.

sections.heading: "Person"
sections.text: The word "person" includes any Company or Association or body of persons, whether incorporated or not.
ingredients: Natural persons
Any Company or Association or body of persons
Whether incorporated or not
sections.key_principle: 'Person' is not confined to human beings — companies and associations can be 'persons' under the Code (relevant to corporate criminal liability).

sections.heading: "Public"
sections.text: The word "public" includes any class of the public or any community.
ingredients: Any class of the public
Any community
sections.key_principle: 'Public' need not mean the whole populace — a section or community suffices.

sections.heading: Definition of "Queen"
sections.text: [Definition of "Queen".] Omitted by the A. O. 1950.
sections.key_principle: Omitted by the Adaptation of Laws Order, 1950 after India became a Republic.
sections.amendment_note: Omitted by the A.O. 1950.

sections.heading: "Servant of Government"
sections.text: The words "servant of Government" denote any officer or servant continued, appointed or employed in India by or under the authority of Government.
ingredients: Officer or servant
Continued, appointed or employed in India
By or under the authority of Government
sections.key_principle: Defines a Government servant by reference to appointment or employment under Government authority; substituted by the A.O. 1950.

footnotes.note_text: Subs., ibid. (A.O. 1950), for section 14.

sections.heading: Definition of "British India"
sections.text: [Definition of "British India".] Rep. by the A. O. 1937.
sections.key_principle: Repealed by the Adaptation of Indian Laws Order, 1937.

sections.heading: Definition of "Government of India"
sections.text: [Definition of "Government of India".] Rep., ibid.
sections.key_principle: Repealed by the Adaptation of Indian Laws Order, 1937.

sections.heading: "Government"
sections.text: The word "Government" denotes the Central Government or the Government of a State.
ingredients: Central Government; OR
Government of a State
sections.key_principle: After 1950 'Government' means the Union or a State Government; the earlier reference to 'Part A' States was omitted by Act 3 of 1951.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by the A.O. 1950, for section 17.
The word and letter 'Part A' omitted by Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch.

sections.heading: "India"
sections.text: "India" means the territory of India excluding the State of Jammu and Kashmir.
ingredients: Territory of India
(as printed) excluding the State of Jammu and Kashmir
sections.key_principle: Definition of 'India' as printed in the source (substituted by Act 3 of 1951); the exclusion of Jammu and Kashmir is now obsolete after Act 34 of 2019 (w.e.f. 31-10-2019), which also omitted the corresponding words in section 1.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by s. 3 and the Sch., ibid., for s. 18 which was ins. by the A.O. 1950. The Original s. 18 was rep. by the A.O. 1937.

sections.heading: "Judge"
sections.text: The word "Judge" denotes not only every person who is officially designated as a Judge, but also every person who is empowered by law to give, in any legal proceeding, civil or criminal, a definitive judgment, or a judgment which, if not appealed against, would be definitive, or a judgment which, if confirmed by some other authority, would be definitive, or who is one of a body of persons, which body of persons is empowered by law to give such a judgment.
ingredients: Person officially designated a Judge; OR
Person empowered by law to give a definitive judgment in civil or criminal proceedings; OR
Person empowered to give a judgment which would be definitive if not appealed against; OR
Person empowered to give a judgment which would be definitive if confirmed by another authority; OR
Member of a body empowered by law to give such a judgment
sections.key_principle: Functional test: a 'Judge' is anyone empowered to give a definitive judgment (or one that would become definitive), regardless of title. A Magistrate who can only commit for trial is NOT a Judge.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A Collector exercising jurisdiction in a suit under Act 10 of 1859, is a Judge.
illustrations.key_principle: Exercising adjudicatory power in a suit makes an executive officer a Judge.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A Magistrate exercising jurisdiction in respect of a charge on which he has power to sentence to fine or imprisonment, with or without appeal, is a Judge.
illustrations.key_principle: Power to pass a sentence (appealable or not) is enough.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A member of a panchayat which has power, under Regulation VII, 1816, of the Madras Code, to try and determine suits, is a Judge.
illustrations.key_principle: A member of a body empowered to give a definitive judgment is a Judge (the Regulation was repealed by Act 3 of 1873).

illustrations.label: Illustration (d)
illustrations.text: A Magistrate exercising jurisdiction in respect of a charge on which he has power only to commit for trial to another Court, is not a Judge.
illustrations.key_principle: A committing Magistrate does not give a definitive judgment, hence is not a 'Judge'.

footnotes.note_text: Rep. by the Madras Civil Courts Act, 1873 (3 of 1873).

sections.heading: "Court of Justice"
sections.text: The words "Court of Justice" denote a Judge who is empowered by law to act judicially alone, or a body of Judges which is empowered by law to act judicially as a body, when such Judge or body of Judges is acting judicially.
ingredients: A Judge empowered by law to act judicially alone; OR
A body of Judges empowered to act judicially as a body
Acting judicially at the time
sections.key_principle: A 'Court of Justice' is defined by function — a Judge or body of Judges acting judicially — not by the building or title.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A Panchayat acting under Regulation VII, 1816, of the Madras Code, having power to try and determine suits, is a Court of Justice.
illustrations.key_principle: A panchayat empowered to try suits is a Court of Justice when acting judicially.

sections.heading: "Public servant"
sections.text: The words "public servant" denote a person falling under any of the descriptions hereinafter following, namely:— [Second to Twelfth clauses as set out below].
ingredients: Person falling within any one of the twelve (originally eleven) descriptions in clauses Second–Twelfth

clauses.text: [Omitted by the A.O. 1950.]
Every Commissioned Officer in the Military, Naval or Air Forces of India.
Every Judge including any person empowered by law to discharge, whether by himself or as a member of any body of persons, any adjudicatory functions.

Every officer of a Court of Justice (including a liquidator, receiver or commissioner) whose duty it is, as such officer, to investigate or report on any matter of law or fact, or to make, authenticate, or keep any document, or to take charge or dispose of any property, or to execute any judicial process, or to administer any oath, or to interpret, or to preserve order in the Court, and every person specially authorised by a Court of Justice to perform any of such duties.
Every juryman, assessor, or member of a panchayat assisting a Court of Justice or public servant.
Every arbitrator or other person to whom any cause or matter has been referred for decision or report by any Court of Justice, or by any other competent public authority.
Every person who holds any office by virtue of which he is empowered to place or keep any person in confinement.

Every officer of the Government whose duty it is, as such officer, to prevent offences, to give information of offences, to bring offenders to justice, or to protect the public health, safety or convenience.

Every officer whose duty it is as such officer, to take, receive, keep or expend any property on behalf of the Government, or to make any survey, assessment or contract on behalf of the Government, or to execute any revenue-process, or to investigate, or to report, on any matter affecting the pecuniary interests of the Government, or to make, authenticate or keep any document relating to the pecuniary interests of the Government, or to prevent the infraction of any law for the protection of the pecuniary interests of the Government.

Every officer whose duty it is, as such officer, to take, receive, keep or expend any property, to make any survey or assessment or to levy any rate or tax for any secular common purpose of any village, town or district, or to make, authenticate or keep any document for the ascertaining of the rights of the people of any village, town or district.
Every person who holds any office in virtue of which he is empowered to prepare, publish, maintain or revise an electoral roll or to conduct an election or part of an election.

Every person— (a) in the service or pay of the Government or remunerated by fees or commission for the performance of any public duty by the Government; (b) in the service or pay of a local authority, a corporation established by or under a Central, Provincial or State Act or a Government company as defined in section 617 of the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956).

sections.key_principle: Central definition for offences by/against public servants (Chapters IX, X etc.). Key tests: duty-based descriptions, actual possession of office is enough (Explanation 2), appointment by Government not required (Explanation 1). Clause 'First' omitted by the A.O. 1950.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A Municipal Commissioner is a public servant.
illustrations.key_principle: An officer of a local authority falls within clause Twelfth(b).

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: Persons falling under any of the above descriptions are public servants, whether appointed by the Government or not.
explanations.plain_language: Government appointment is not necessary — the nature of the duty/office decides.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: Wherever the words "public servant" occur, they shall be understood of every person who is in actual possession of the situation of a public servant, whatever legal defect there may be in his right to hold that situation.
explanations.plain_language: A de facto public servant is covered even if his appointment is legally defective.

explanations.label: Explanation 3
explanations.text: The word "election" denotes an election for the purpose of selecting members of any legislative, municipal or other public authority, of whatever character, the method of selection to which is by, or under, any law prescribed as by election.
explanations.plain_language: 'Election' covers any legally prescribed election to a legislative, municipal or other public body.

state_amendments.text: After clause Twelfth, the following new clause is added: "Thirteenth.—Every person employed or engaged by any public body in the conduct and supervision of any examination recognised or approved under any law." Explanation.—The expression "Public Body" includes (a) a University, Board of Education or other body, either established by or under a Central or State Act or under the provisions of the Constitution of India or constituted by the Government; and (b) a local authority.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by the A.O. 1950, for 'the Crown' which had been subs. by the A.O. 1937, for 'Government'.
Certain words omitted by Act 40 of 1964, s. 2.
Ins. by Act 39 of 1920, s. 2 (clause Eleventh and Explanation 3).
Subs. by Act 40 of 1964, s. 2, for Cl. Twelfth.
Explanation 4 omitted by Act 39 of 1920, s. 2.
Subs. by Act 10 of 1927, s. 2 and the First Sch., for 'or Naval'.
Subs. by Act 40 of 1964, s. 2, for cl. Third.
Ins. by s. 2, ibid. (Act 40 of 1964).

sections.heading: "Movable property"
sections.text: The words "movable property" are intended to include corporeal property of every description, except land and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything which is attached to the earth.
ingredients: Corporeal (tangible) property of every description
Excludes land
Excludes things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth
sections.key_principle: Only tangible, severable property is 'movable' — key to theft, extortion and misappropriation (Chapter XVII). Land and fixtures are excluded until severed.

sections.heading: "Wrongful gain" / "Wrongful loss"
sections.text: "Wrongful gain" is gain by unlawful means of property to which the person gaining is not legally entitled. "Wrongful loss" is the loss by unlawful means of property to which the person losing it is legally entitled.
ingredients: Wrongful gain: gain by unlawful means
Of property to which the gainer is not legally entitled
Wrongful loss: loss by unlawful means
Of property to which the loser is legally entitled
sections.key_principle: Both 'unlawful means' and absence/presence of legal entitlement are required. Building block for 'dishonestly' (s. 24).

explanations.label: Gaining wrongfully / Losing wrongfully
explanations.text: A person is said to gain wrongfully when such person retains wrongfully, as well as when such person acquires wrongfully. A person is said to lose wrongfully when such person is wrongfully kept out of any property, as well as when such person is wrongfully deprived of property.
explanations.plain_language: Wrongful gain/loss covers wrongful retention and being wrongfully kept out of property, not merely initial acquisition or deprivation.

sections.heading: "Dishonestly"
sections.text: Whoever does anything with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another person, is said to do that thing "dishonestly".
ingredients: Doing anything
With the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person; OR
With the intention of causing wrongful loss to another person
sections.key_principle: Dishonesty depends on intention to cause wrongful gain OR wrongful loss — either suffices (s. 23). Central mens rea for theft, misappropriation, breach of trust and similar offences.

sections.heading: "Fraudulently"
sections.text: A person is said to do a thing fraudulently if he does that thing with intent to defraud but not otherwise.
ingredients: Doing a thing
With intent to defraud
sections.key_principle: 'Fraudulently' requires intent to defraud — deception coupled with injury/advantage; mere dishonesty is distinct (s. 24).

sections.heading: "Reason to believe"
sections.text: A person is said to have "reason to believe" a thing, if he has sufficient cause to believe that thing but not otherwise.
ingredients: Sufficient cause to believe the thing
sections.key_principle: Objective standard — sufficient cause, not mere suspicion; weaker than actual knowledge but stronger than suspicion.

sections.heading: "Property in possession of wife, clerk or servant"
sections.text: When property is in the possession of a person's wife, clerk or servant, on account of that person, it is in that person's possession within the meaning of this Code.
ingredients: Property held by wife, clerk or servant
Held on account of the master/husband
sections.key_principle: Constructive possession: the possession of a wife, clerk or servant on behalf of the owner is the owner's possession — crucial to theft (s. 378) and breach of trust.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: A person employed temporarily or on a particular occasion in the capacity of a clerk or servant, is a clerk or servant within the meaning of this section.
explanations.plain_language: Temporary or occasional clerks and servants are covered.

sections.heading: "Counterfeit"
sections.text: A person is said to "counterfeit" who causes one thing to resemble another thing, intending by means of that resemblance to practise deception, or knowing it to be likely that deception will thereby be practised.
ingredients: Causing one thing to resemble another
Intending to practise deception; OR
Knowing it likely that deception will be practised
sections.key_principle: Counterfeiting needs resemblance plus deceptive intention/knowledge; exact imitation is unnecessary.

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: It is not essential to counterfeiting that the imitation should be exact.
explanations.plain_language: A rough imitation can still be counterfeiting.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: When a person causes one thing to resemble another thing, and the resemblance is such that a person might be deceived thereby, it shall be presumed, until the contrary is proved, that the person so causing the one thing to resemble the other thing intended by means of that resemblance to practise deception or knew it to be likely that deception would thereby be practised.
explanations.plain_language: Rebuttable presumption of deceptive intention where the resemblance could deceive.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 1 of 1889, s. 9, for the Explanation.

sections.heading: "Document"
sections.text: The word "document" denotes any matter expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters, figures or marks, or by more than one of those means, intended to be used, or which may be used, as evidence of that matter.
ingredients: Matter expressed or described upon any substance
By letters, figures or marks (or more than one)
Intended to be used, or which may be used, as evidence of that matter
sections.key_principle: Broad, substance-neutral definition — what matters is that the marks may serve as evidence. Basis of forgery offences (Chapter XVIII).

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A writing expressing the terms of a contract, which may be used as evidence of the contract, is a document.
illustrations.key_principle: Writing capable of serving as evidence of a contract is a document.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A cheque upon a banker is a document.
illustrations.key_principle: A cheque is a document.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A power-of-attorney is a document.
illustrations.key_principle: A power-of-attorney is a document.

illustrations.label: Illustration (d)
illustrations.text: A map or plan which is intended to be used or which may be used as evidence, is a document.
illustrations.key_principle: Maps and plans are documents if usable as evidence.

illustrations.label: Illustration (e)
illustrations.text: A writing containing directions or instructions is a document.
illustrations.key_principle: Instructions in writing are documents.

illustrations.label: Illustration (f) [under Explanation 2]
illustrations.text: A writes his name on the back of a bill of exchange payable to his order. The meaning of the endorsement, as explained by mercantile usage, is that the bill is to be paid to the holder. The endorsement is a document, and must be construed in the same manner as if the words "pay to the holder" or words to that effect had been written over the signature.
illustrations.key_principle: Mercantile usage supplies the meaning of what is written (Explanation 2).

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: It is immaterial by what means or upon what substance the letters, figures or marks are formed, or whether the evidence is intended for, or may be used in, a Court of Justice, or not.
explanations.plain_language: Medium and intended forum are irrelevant.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: Whatever is expressed by means of letters, figures or marks as explained by mercantile or other usage, shall be deemed to be expressed by such letters, figures or marks within the meaning of this section, although the same may not be actually expressed.
explanations.plain_language: Meaning conveyed by trade/mercantile usage counts as part of the document.

sections.heading: "Electronic record"
sections.text: The words "electronic record" shall have the meaning assigned to them in clause (t) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2000).
sections.inserted_by: Act 21 of 2000, s. 91 and the First Sch. (w.e.f. 17-10-2000)
ingredients: Meaning taken from s. 2(1)(t) of the Information Technology Act, 2000
sections.key_principle: Imports the IT Act definition so that electronic records can be treated as documents for forgery and related offences.

footnotes.note_text: Ins. by Act 21 of 2000, s. 91 and the First Sch. (w.e.f. 17-10-2000).

sections.heading: "Valuable security"
sections.text: The words "valuable security" denote a document which is, or purports to be, a document whereby any legal right is created, extended, transferred, restricted, extinguished or released, or whereby any person acknowledges that he lies under legal liability, or has not a certain legal right.
ingredients: A document which is, or purports to be, one whereby a legal right is created, extended, transferred, restricted, extinguished or released; OR
A document whereby a person acknowledges legal liability or absence of a legal right
sections.key_principle: A document that affects legal rights or liabilities. Important for aggravated forgery, cheating and breach of trust provisions.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A writes his name on the back of a bill of exchange. As the effect of this endorsement is to transfer the right to the bill to any person who may become the unlawful holder of it, the endorsement is a "valuable security".
illustrations.key_principle: An endorsement that transfers rights in a bill is a valuable security.

sections.heading: "A will"
sections.text: The words "a will" denote any testamentary document.
ingredients: Any testamentary document
sections.key_principle: Wide definition of a will — any testamentary document.

sections.heading: Words referring to acts include illegal omissions
sections.text: In every part of this Code, except where a contrary intention appears from the context, words which refer to acts done extend also to illegal omissions.
ingredients: Words referring to acts done
Extend to illegal omissions
Unless a contrary intention appears
sections.key_principle: Offences defined by 'act' include illegal omissions (failure to do what one is legally bound to do — see s. 43).

sections.heading: "Act". "Omission".
sections.text: The word "act" denotes as well a series of acts as a single act: the word "omission" denotes as well a series of omissions as a single omission.
ingredients: 'Act' = a single act or a series of acts
'Omission' = a single omission or a series of omissions
sections.key_principle: Acts and omissions may be single or continuous series.

sections.heading: Acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention
sections.text: When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone.
ingredients: Criminal act
Done by several persons
In furtherance of the common intention of all
Each liable as if he alone did it
sections.key_principle: Joint liability rule — it creates no substantive offence but fixes constructive liability. Requires (i) a criminal act, (ii) a common intention shared by all (pre-arranged plan, may form on the spot) and (iii) participation in the act.
sections.amendment_note: Section substituted by Act 27 of 1870, s. 1, for original section 34.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 27 of 1870, s. 1, for section 34.

sections.heading: When such an act is criminal by reason of its being done with a criminal knowledge or intention
sections.text: Whenever an act, which is criminal only by reason of its being done with a criminal knowledge or intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act with such knowledge or intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act were done by him alone with that knowledge or intention.
ingredients: Act criminal only because of criminal knowledge or intention
Done by several persons
Each who joins with that knowledge or intention is liable as if he alone did it
sections.key_principle: Liability attaches only to those participants who share the requisite guilty knowledge/intention; an innocent participant is not liable.

sections.heading: Effect caused partly by act and partly by omission
sections.text: Wherever the causing of a certain effect, or an attempt to cause that effect, by an act or by an omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by an omission is the same offence.
ingredients: Effect (or attempt) is an offence if caused by act or omission
Partly act and partly omission is the same offence
sections.key_principle: A mixed act/omission course of conduct is treated as the same offence.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A intentionally causes Z's death, partly by illegally omitting to give Z food, and partly by beating Z. A has committed murder.
illustrations.key_principle: Death caused by a combination of illegal omission and act is murder.

sections.heading: Co-operation by doing one of several acts constituting an offence
sections.text: When an offence is committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally co-operates in the commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, commits that offence.
ingredients: Offence committed by several acts
Intentional co-operation
By doing any one of those acts, singly or jointly
sections.key_principle: Each person who intentionally does one of the several acts constituting the offence is guilty of the whole offence.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A and B agree to murder Z by severally and at different times giving him small doses of poison. A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty of the offence though their acts are separate.
illustrations.verdict: A and B both guilty of murder
illustrations.key_principle: Separate acts, in intentional co-operation, each make the actor guilty of the whole offence.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z's death, knowingly co-operate in causing that effect by illegally omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose. Z dies of hunger. Both A and B are guilty of the murder of Z.
illustrations.verdict: A and B both guilty of murder
illustrations.key_principle: Co-operation can be by omissions as well as acts.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z's death, illegally omits to supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or co-operation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z's death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not co-operate with B, A is guilty only of an attempt to commit murder.
illustrations.verdict: B = murder; A = attempt to murder
illustrations.key_principle: Without co-operation or collusion each is liable only for his own part.

sections.heading: Persons concerned in criminal act may be guilty of different offences
sections.text: Where several persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be guilty of different offences by means of that act.
ingredients: Several persons engaged in a criminal act
Each may be guilty of a different offence depending on his own intention/knowledge
sections.key_principle: Liability depends on each person's individual mens rea, so co-participants can be convicted of different offences from the same act.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A attacks Z under such circumstances of grave provocation that his killing of Z would be only culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged in causing Z's death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide.
illustrations.key_principle: Provocation benefits only the provoked person; the participant with independent murderous intent is guilty of murder.

sections.heading: "Voluntarily"
sections.text: A person is said to cause an effect "voluntarily" when he causes it by means whereby he intended to cause it, or by means which, at the time of employing those means, he knew or had reason to believe to be likely to cause it.
ingredients: Causes an effect by means intended to cause it; OR
By means which he knew to be likely to cause it; OR
By means which he had reason to believe likely to cause it

mens_rea_modes.description: Intention to cause the effect
Knowledge that the means are likely to cause the effect
Reason to believe the means are likely to cause the effect

sections.key_principle: 'Voluntarily' includes foreseen consequences — not only intended ones. Even if the person is sorry about the result, he acts voluntarily if he knew it was likely.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A sets fire, by night, to an inhabited house in a large town, for the purpose of facilitating a robbery and thus causes the death of a person. Here, A may not have intended to cause death; and may even be sorry that death has been caused by his act; yet, if he knew that he was likely to cause death, he has caused death voluntarily.
illustrations.key_principle: Knowledge of likelihood of death makes the causing 'voluntary' even without intent.

sections.heading: "Offence"
sections.text: Except in the Chapters and sections mentioned in clauses 2 and 3 of this section, the word "offence" denotes a thing made punishable by this Code. In Chapter IV, Chapter VA and in the following sections, namely, sections 64, 65, 66, 67, 71, 109, 110, 112, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119 and 120, 187, 194, 195, 203, 211, 213, 214, 221, 222, 223, 224, 225, 327, 328, 329, 330, 331, 347, 348, 388, 389 and 445, the word "offence" denotes a thing punishable under this Code, or under any special or local law as hereinafter defined. And in sections 141, 176, 177, 201, 202, 212, 216 and 441, the word "offence" has the same meaning when the thing punishable under the special or local law is punishable under such law with imprisonment for a term of six months or upwards, whether with or without fine.
ingredients: General rule: offence = thing made punishable by this Code
Extended sense in Chapter IV, Chapter VA and listed sections: also punishable under any special or local law
Narrower extended sense in sections 141, 176, 177, 201, 202, 212, 216 and 441: special/local-law offence punishable with imprisonment of six months or upwards
sections.key_principle: Three-tier definition of 'offence'. In most places it means an IPC offence; in listed sections it extends to special/local law offences; in a further listed group only to special/local-law offences carrying at least six months' imprisonment.
sections.amendment_note: Section substituted by Act 27 of 1870, s. 2; 'Chapters' substituted by Act 8 of 1930; Chapter VA inserted by Act 8 of 1913; section 64–67 and 71 inserted by Act 8 of 1882 and Act 10 of 1886; ss. 118, 119 and 120 inserted by Act 10 of 2009 (w.e.f. 27-10-2009).

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 27 of 1870, s. 2, for section 40.
Subs. by Act 8 of 1930, s. 2 and the First Sch., for 'Chapter'.
Ins. by Act 8 of 1913, s. 2.
Ins. by Act 8 of 1882, s. 1.
Ins. by Act 10 of 1886, s. 21 (1).

sections.heading: "Special law"
sections.text: A "special law" is a law applicable to a particular subject.
ingredients: A law applicable to a particular subject
sections.key_principle: Subject-matter test (e.g. the Arms Act, NDPS Act).

sections.heading: "Local law"
sections.text: A "local law" is a law applicable only to a particular part of India.
ingredients: A law applicable only to a particular part of India
sections.key_principle: Territorial test — contrasts with a special law, which is subject-based.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by the A.O. 1948, for 'British India'.
The words 'the territories comprised in' omitted by Act 48 of 1952, s. 3 and the Second Sch.
Subs. by Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch., for 'the States' which had been subs. by the A.O. 1950, for 'the Provinces'.

sections.heading: "Illegal". "Legally bound to do".
sections.text: The word "illegal" is applicable to everything which is an offence or which is prohibited by law, or which furnishes ground for a civil action; and a person is said to be "legally bound to do" whatever it is illegal in him to omit.
ingredients: Illegal = an offence; OR prohibited by law; OR furnishes ground for a civil action
Legally bound to do = whatever it is illegal to omit
sections.key_principle: 'Illegal' covers crimes, prohibitions and civil wrongs; an illegal omission is a failure to do what one is legally bound to do (links to s. 32).

sections.heading: "Injury"
sections.text: The word "injury" denotes any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.
ingredients: Any harm whatever
Illegally caused
To body, mind, reputation or property
sections.key_principle: Four heads of injury — body, mind, reputation, property — each must be illegally caused.

sections.heading: "Life"
sections.text: The word "life" denotes the life of a human being, unless the contrary appears from the context.
ingredients: Life of a human being
sections.key_principle: 'Life' is human life unless context shows otherwise.

sections.heading: "Death"
sections.text: The word "death" denotes the death of a human being unless the contrary appears from the context.
ingredients: Death of a human being
sections.key_principle: 'Death' is human death unless context shows otherwise.

sections.heading: "Animal"
sections.text: The word "animal" denotes any living creature, other than a human being.
ingredients: Any living creature
Other than a human being
sections.key_principle: Animals are living creatures other than humans (relevant to mischief and cruelty offences).

sections.heading: "Vessel"
sections.text: The word "vessel" denotes anything made for the conveyance by water of human beings or of property.
ingredients: Anything made for conveyance by water
Of human beings or of property
sections.key_principle: Purpose-based definition — anything made for carrying persons or property by water.

sections.heading: "Year". "Month".
sections.text: Wherever the word "year" or the word "month" is used, it is to be understood that the year or the month is to be reckoned according to the British calendar.
ingredients: 'Year' and 'month' are reckoned by the British (Gregorian) calendar
sections.key_principle: Calendar months and years, not lunar or 30-day months.

sections.heading: "Section"
sections.text: The word "section" denotes one of those portions of a Chapter of this Code which are distinguished by prefixed numeral figures.
ingredients: A portion of a Chapter distinguished by prefixed numeral figures
sections.key_principle: Defines 'section' by its numbered form.

sections.heading: "Oath"
sections.text: The word "oath" includes a solemn affirmation substituted by law for an oath, and any declaration required or authorised by law to be made before a public servant or to be used for the purpose of proof, whether in a Court of Justice or not.
ingredients: Oath proper
Solemn affirmation substituted by law for an oath
Any declaration required or authorised by law to be made before a public servant
Any declaration to be used for proof, in a Court or not
sections.key_principle: Broad definition — includes affirmations and statutory declarations (relevant to false evidence offences).

sections.heading: "Good faith"
sections.text: Nothing is said to be done or believed in "good faith" which is done or believed without due care and attention.
ingredients: Act done or believed
With due care and attention
sections.key_principle: Objective test of good faith — due care and attention, not merely honest belief. Many exceptions and defences depend on it.

sections.heading: "Harbour"
sections.text: Except in section 157, and in section 130 in the case in which the harbour is given by the wife or husband of the person harboured, the word "harbour" includes the supplying a person with shelter, food, drink, money, clothes, arms, ammunition or means of conveyance, or the assisting a person by any means, whether of the same kind as those enumerated in this section or not, to evade apprehension.
ingredients: Supplying shelter, food, drink, money, clothes, arms, ammunition or means of conveyance; OR
Assisting a person by any other means to evade apprehension
Exceptions: s. 157 and s. 130 (where the harbour is given by the wife/husband of the person harboured) have their own scope
sections.key_principle: Broad, non-exhaustive definition of 'harbouring' — any assistance to evade apprehension. Spousal harbouring is carved out of s. 130 (aiding escape of State prisoner).

footnotes.note_text: Ins. by Act 8 of 1942, s. 2.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Punishments

chapters_covered: III — Of Punishments
key_themes: Exhaustive list of punishments: death, life imprisonment, rigorous/simple imprisonment, forfeiture, fine (s. 53)
Abolition of transportation and its replacement by imprisonment for life (ss. 53, 53A, 58, 59)
Commutation of death and life sentences by the appropriate Government (ss. 54, 55, 55A)
Life imprisonment reckoned as 20 years only for fractions (s. 57)
Fine: amount (s. 63), default imprisonment and its limits (ss. 64–69), recovery period (s. 70)
Limit of punishment for composite or overlapping offences (s. 71) and doubtful offences (s. 72)
Solitary confinement — scale and execution limits (ss. 73–74)
Enhanced punishment for repeat property/coin offences (s. 75)
notable_amendments: Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 — 'transportation' replaced by 'imprisonment for life'; ss. 58–59 repealed; s. 53A inserted (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).
Act 17 of 1949 — clause Thirdly (penal servitude) of s. 53 and s. 56 omitted/repealed (w.e.f. 6-4-1949).
Act 16 of 1921, s. 4 — ss. 61 and 62 (forfeiture of property) repealed.
Act 8 of 1882 and Act 10 of 1886 — ss. 64 and 67 amended on default imprisonment.
Act 3 of 1910, s. 2 — s. 75 substituted; Act 3 of 1951 — clause (b) omitted.
metadata.case_query: A convict is fined ₹50,000 for an offence carrying a maximum of 2 years' imprisonment with fine; the court directs 2 years' imprisonment in default of payment. He argues that the default term is excessive.

sections.heading: Punishments
sections.text: The punishments to which offenders are liable under the provisions of this Code are— First.—Death; Secondly.—Imprisonment for life; Thirdly.—[Omitted]; Fourthly.—Imprisonment, which is of two descriptions, namely: (1) Rigorous, that is, with hard labour; (2) Simple; Fifthly.—Forfeiture of property; Sixthly.—Fine.
ingredients: Death
Imprisonment for life
Imprisonment — rigorous (with hard labour) or simple
Forfeiture of property
Fine
sections.key_principle: Exhaustive list of the punishments under the Code. 'Transportation' (Secondly) was replaced by 'imprisonment for life' in 1955; clause Thirdly (penal servitude) was omitted in 1949.
sections.amendment_note: Clause 'Secondly' substituted by Act 26 of 1955 (w.e.f. 1-1-1956); clause 'Thirdly' omitted by Act 17 of 1949 (w.e.f. 6-4-1949).

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'Secondly.—Transportation' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).
Cl. Thirdly omitted by Act 17 of 1949, s. 2 (w.e.f. 6-4-1949).

sections.heading: Construction of reference to transportation
sections.text: (1) Subject to the provisions of sub-section (2) and sub-section (3), any reference to "transportation for life" in any other law for the time being in force or in any instrument or order having effect by virtue of any such law or of any enactment repealed shall be construed as a reference to "imprisonment for life". (2) In every case in which a sentence of transportation for a term has been passed before the commencement of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1955 (26 of 1955), the offender shall be dealt with in the same manner as if sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for the same term. (3) Any reference to transportation for a term or to transportation for any shorter term (by whatever name called) in any other law for the time being in force shall be deemed to have been omitted. (4) Any reference to "transportation" in any other law for the time being in force shall,— (a) if the expression means transportation for life, be construed as a reference to imprisonment for life; (b) if the expression means transportation for any shorter term, be deemed to have been omitted.
sections.inserted_by: Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956)
ingredients: Transportation for life = imprisonment for life
Earlier sentences of transportation for a term = rigorous imprisonment for the same term
References to transportation for a term in other laws deemed omitted
sections.key_principle: Transitional/construction provision following abolition of transportation in 1955.

subsections.text: Any reference to "transportation for life" in any other law shall be construed as a reference to "imprisonment for life".
Pre-1955 sentences of transportation for a term are treated as rigorous imprisonment for the same term.
References to transportation for a term in other laws are deemed omitted.
Other references to 'transportation': (a) for life → imprisonment for life; (b) for a shorter term → deemed omitted.

footnotes.note_text: Ins. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).
Subs. by Act 36 of 1957, s. 3 and the Second Sch., for '1954'.

sections.heading: Commutation of sentence of death
sections.text: In every case in which sentence of death shall have been passed, the appropriate Government may, without the consent of the offender, commute the punishment for any other punishment provided by this Code.
ingredients: Sentence of death has been passed
Appropriate Government may commute it
Without the offender's consent
To any other punishment provided by the Code
sections.key_principle: Executive power of commutation of death sentence — consent of the offender is not needed. Defined 'appropriate Government' in s. 55A.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by the A.O. 1950, for 'the Central Government or the Provincial Government of the Province within which the offender shall have been sentenced'.

sections.heading: Commutation of sentence of imprisonment for life
sections.text: In every case in which sentence of imprisonment for life shall have been passed, the appropriate Government may, without the consent of the offender, commute the punishment for imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding fourteen years.
ingredients: Sentence of imprisonment for life
Appropriate Government may commute
Without the offender's consent
To imprisonment of either description not exceeding fourteen years
sections.key_principle: Life imprisonment may be commuted to a maximum of 14 years' imprisonment of either description.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).
Subs. by the A.O. 1950, for 'the Provincial Government of the Province within which the offender shall have been sentenced'.

sections.heading: Definition of "appropriate Government"
sections.text: In sections fifty-four and fifty-five the expression "appropriate Government" means,— (a) in cases where the sentence is a sentence of death or is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends, the Central Government; and (b) in cases where the sentence (whether of death or not) is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends, the Government of the State within which the offender is sentenced.
ingredients: Central Government: death sentences, or offences against laws on Union-executive matters
State Government: offences against laws on State-executive matters, where the offender is sentenced
sections.key_principle: Allocates the commutation power between Union and State according to the executive power over the subject-matter of the law; death sentences are always the Central Government's.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by the A.O. 1950. Earlier ins by the A.O. 1937.

sections.heading: Sentence of Europeans and Americans to penal servitude. Proviso as to sentence for term exceeding ten years but not for life.
sections.text: [Sentence of Europeans and Americans to penal servitude. Proviso as to sentence for term exceeding ten years but not for life.] Rep. by the Criminal Law (Removal of Racial Discriminations) Act, 1949 (17 of 1949) (w.e.f. 6-4-1949).
sections.repealed_by: Criminal Law (Removal of Racial Discriminations) Act, 1949 (17 of 1949), w.e.f. 6-4-1949
sections.key_principle: Repealed — racial distinction in sentencing removed in 1949.

sections.heading: Fractions of terms of punishment
sections.text: In calculating fractions of terms of punishment, imprisonment for life shall be reckoned as equivalent to imprisonment for twenty years.
ingredients: Calculating fractions of terms of punishment
Imprisonment for life reckoned as 20 years
sections.key_principle: A computational rule only (e.g. for working out one-fourth in s. 65, remission fractions). It does NOT mean life imprisonment is limited to 20 years — a life convict serves life unless remitted/commuted.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Offenders sentenced to transportation how dealt with until transported
sections.text: [Offenders sentenced to transportation how dealt with until transported.] Rep. by the Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1955 (26 of 1955), s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).
sections.repealed_by: Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956)
sections.key_principle: Repealed on abolition of transportation.

sections.heading: Transportation instead of imprisonment
sections.text: [Transportation instead of imprisonment.] Rep. by s. 117 and the Sch., ibid. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).
sections.repealed_by: Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956)
sections.key_principle: Repealed on abolition of transportation.

sections.heading: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple
sections.text: In every case in which an offender is punishable with imprisonment which may be of either description, it shall be competent to the Court which sentences such offender to direct in the sentence that such imprisonment shall be wholly rigorous, or that such imprisonment shall be wholly simple, or that any part of such imprisonment shall be rigorous and the rest simple.
ingredients: Offence punishable with imprisonment of either description
Court may direct wholly rigorous; OR wholly simple; OR part rigorous and part simple
sections.key_principle: Court's discretion to choose the character of imprisonment where the section allows 'either description'.

sections.heading: Sentence of forfeiture of property
sections.text: [Sentence of forfeiture of property.] Rep. by the Indian Penal Code (Amendment) Act, 1921 (16 of 1921), s. 4.
sections.repealed_by: Indian Penal Code (Amendment) Act, 1921 (16 of 1921), s. 4
sections.key_principle: Repealed in 1921.

sections.heading: Forfeiture of property, in respect of offenders punishable with death, transportation or imprisonment
sections.text: [Forfeiture of property, in respect of offenders punishable with death, transportation or imprisonment.] Rep. by s. 4 ibid.
sections.repealed_by: Indian Penal Code (Amendment) Act, 1921 (16 of 1921), s. 4
sections.key_principle: Repealed in 1921.

sections.heading: Amount of fine
sections.text: Where no sum is expressed to which a fine may extend, the amount of fine to which the offender is liable is unlimited, but shall not be excessive.
ingredients: No sum expressed as maximum fine
Fine is unlimited
But must not be excessive
sections.key_principle: Where the section prescribes only 'fine', the amount is discretionary but must be reasonable in the circumstances.

sections.heading: Sentence of imprisonment for non-payment of fine
sections.text: In every case of an offence punishable with imprisonment as well as fine, in which the offender is sentenced to a fine, whether with or without imprisonment, and in every case of an offence punishable with imprisonment or fine, or with fine only, in which the offender is sentenced to a fine, it shall be competent to the Court which sentences such offender to direct by the sentence that, in default of payment of the fine, the offender shall suffer imprisonment for a certain term, which imprisonment shall be in excess of any other imprisonment to which he may have been sentenced or to which he may be liable under a commutation of a sentence.
ingredients: Offence punishable with imprisonment and fine; OR imprisonment or fine; OR fine only
Offender sentenced to a fine
Court may direct imprisonment in default of payment
Default imprisonment is additional to any other imprisonment
sections.key_principle: Default sentence: the Court may order imprisonment in default of payment of fine; it runs in addition to the substantive sentence.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 8 of 1882, s. 2, for 'In every case in which an offender is sentenced to a fine'.
Ins. by Act 10 of 1886, s. 21 (2).

sections.heading: Limit to imprisonment for non-payment of fine, when imprisonment and fine awardable
sections.text: The term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned in default of payment of a fine shall not exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment which is the maximum fixed for the offence, if the offence be punishable with imprisonment as well as fine.
ingredients: Offence punishable with imprisonment as well as fine
Default term must not exceed one-fourth of the maximum imprisonment for the offence
sections.key_principle: Cap on default sentence — one-fourth of the maximum imprisonment fixed for the offence.

sections.heading: Description of imprisonment for non-payment of fine
sections.text: The imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of a fine may be of any description to which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence.
ingredients: Default imprisonment may be of any description (rigorous or simple) that could have been imposed for the offence
sections.key_principle: Default imprisonment follows the descriptions available for the offence itself.

sections.heading: Imprisonment for non-payment of fine, when offence punishable with fine only
sections.text: If the offence be punishable with fine only, the imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of the fine shall be simple, and the term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned, in default of payment of fine, shall not exceed the following scale, that is to say, for any term not exceeding two months when the amount of the fine shall not exceed fifty rupees, and for any term not exceeding four months when the amount shall not exceed one hundred rupees, and for any term not exceeding six months in any other case.
ingredients: Offence punishable with fine only
Default imprisonment must be simple
Up to 2 months if fine ≤ ₹50
Up to 4 months if fine ≤ ₹100
Up to 6 months in any other case

punishment_options.condition: Up to 2 months where fine does not exceed ₹50
Up to 4 months where fine does not exceed ₹100
Up to 6 months in any other case

sections.key_principle: Graduated scale for default imprisonment where the offence carries only a fine.

footnotes.note_text: Ins. by Act 8 of 1882, s. 3.

sections.heading: Imprisonment to terminate on payment of fine
sections.text: The imprisonment which is imposed in default of payment of a fine shall terminate whenever that fine is either paid or levied by process of law.
ingredients: Default imprisonment terminates when fine is paid; OR levied by process of law
sections.key_principle: Payment (or recovery) of the fine ends the default imprisonment immediately.

sections.heading: Termination of imprisonment on payment of proportional part of fine
sections.text: If, before the expiration of the term of imprisonment fixed in default of payment, such a proportion of the fine be paid or levied that the term of imprisonment suffered in default of payment is not less than proportional to the part of the fine still unpaid, the imprisonment shall terminate.
ingredients: Part-payment of fine made before expiry of the default term
Imprisonment already suffered is not less than proportional to the unpaid portion
Imprisonment terminates
sections.key_principle: Proportional release: part-payment ends default imprisonment once time served is at least proportional to the fine still unpaid.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A is sentenced to a fine of one hundred rupees and to four months' imprisonment in default of payment. Here, if seventy-five rupees of the fine be paid or levied before the expiration of one month of the imprisonment, A will be discharged as soon as the first month has expired. If seventy-five rupees be paid or levied at the time of the expiration of the first month, or at any later time while A continues in imprisonment, A will be immediately discharged. If fifty rupees of the fine be paid or levied before the expiration of two months of the imprisonment, A will be discharged as soon as the two months are completed. If fifty rupees be paid or levied at the time of the expiration of those two months, or at any later time while A continues in imprisonment, A will be immediately discharged.
illustrations.verdict: Discharge once time served is proportional to unpaid fine
illustrations.key_principle: ₹100 fine = 4 months, so each ₹25 = 1 month: paying ₹75 secures release after 1 month; paying ₹50 secures release after 2 months.

sections.heading: Fine leviable within six years, or during imprisonment. Death not to discharge property from liability
sections.text: The fine, or any part thereof which remains unpaid, may be levied at any time within six years after the passing of the sentence, and if, under the sentence, the offender be liable to imprisonment for a longer period than six years, then at any time previous to the expiration of that period; and the death of the offender does not discharge from the liability any property which would, after his death, be legally liable for his debts.
ingredients: Unpaid fine may be levied within six years of sentence
Or, if sentence exceeds six years, at any time before that longer period expires
Offender's death does not discharge property liable for his debts
sections.key_principle: Limitation of six years (or the sentence length if longer) for recovery of fine; the estate remains liable after death.

sections.heading: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences
sections.text: Where anything which is an offence is made up of parts, any of which parts is itself an offence, the offender shall not be punished with the punishment of more than one of such his offences, unless it be so expressly provided. Where anything is an offence falling within two or more separate definitions of any law in force for the time being by which offences are defined or punished, or where several acts, of which one or more than one would by itself or themselves constitute an offence, constitute, when combined, a different offence, the offender shall not be punished with a more severe punishment than the Court which tries him could award for any one of such offences.
ingredients: Offence made up of parts, any of which is itself an offence — only one punishment
Act falling within two or more definitions of offences — punishment not exceeding the maximum for any one
Several acts which, combined, constitute a different offence — same limit
sections.key_principle: Bar against double punishment for what is substantially a single act (compare Art. 20(2) of the Constitution and s. 300 CrPC). The aggregate punishment is capped at the Court's power for any one of the offences.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A gives Z fifty strokes with a stick. Here A may have committed the offence of voluntarily causing hurt to Z by the whole beating, and also by each of the blows which make up the whole beating. If A were liable to punishment for every blow, he might be imprisoned for fifty years, one for each blow. But he is liable only to one punishment for the whole beating.
illustrations.verdict: One punishment for the whole beating
illustrations.key_principle: An offence made up of parts is punished once, not once for each component.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: But, if, while A is beating Z, Y interferes, and A intentionally strikes Y, here, as the blow given to Y is no part of the act whereby A voluntarily causes hurt to Z, A is liable to one punishment for voluntarily causing hurt to Z, and to another for the blow given to Y.
illustrations.key_principle: The blow to Y is a distinct offence, not part of the beating of Z, so separate punishment follows.

footnotes.note_text: Added by s. 4, ibid. (Act 8 of 1882).

sections.heading: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, the judgment stating that it is doubtful of which
sections.text: In all cases in which judgment is given that a person is guilty of one of several offences specified in the judgment, but that it is doubtful of which of these offences he is guilty, the offender shall be punished for the offence for which the lowest punishment is provided if the same punishment is not provided for all.
ingredients: Judgment finds guilt of one of several specified offences
Doubtful which offence
Punishment is that for the offence carrying the lowest punishment (unless all carry the same)
sections.key_principle: Benefit of doubt in sentencing — when it is uncertain which of several offences was committed, only the lightest punishment can be imposed.

sections.heading: Solitary confinement
sections.text: Whenever any person is convicted of an offence for which under this Code the Court has power to sentence him to rigorous imprisonment, the Court may, by its sentence, order that the offender shall be kept in solitary confinement for any portion or portions of the imprisonment to which he is sentenced, not exceeding three months in the whole, according to the following scale, that is to say— a time not exceeding one month if the term of imprisonment shall not exceed six months; a time not exceeding two months if the term of imprisonment shall exceed six months and shall not exceed one year; a time not exceeding three months if the term of imprisonment shall exceed one year.
ingredients: Conviction for an offence where rigorous imprisonment may be awarded
Court orders solitary confinement for part of the sentence
Maximum three months in the whole, per scale

punishment_options.condition: Up to 1 month — where imprisonment does not exceed 6 months
Up to 2 months — where imprisonment exceeds 6 months but does not exceed 1 year
Up to 3 months — where imprisonment exceeds 1 year

sections.key_principle: Solitary confinement is a permissible part of a rigorous-imprisonment sentence only, subject to the scale; in practice it has been severely restricted by the Supreme Court (Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration).

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 8 of 1862, s. 5, for 'be less than a'.

sections.heading: Limit of solitary confinement
sections.text: In executing a sentence of solitary confinement, such confinement shall in no case exceed fourteen days at a time, with intervals between the periods of solitary confinement of not less duration than such periods; and when the imprisonment awarded shall exceed three months, the solitary confinement shall not exceed seven days in any one month of the whole imprisonment awarded, with intervals between the periods of solitary confinement of not less duration than such periods.
ingredients: Not more than 14 days at a time
Intervals at least equal to the periods of confinement
Where imprisonment exceeds three months — not more than 7 days in any one month
sections.key_principle: Execution limits on solitary confinement: 14 days at a stretch (7 days a month on longer sentences) with equal rest intervals.

sections.heading: Enhanced punishment for certain offences under Chapter XII or Chapter XVII after previous conviction
sections.text: Whoever, having been convicted, by a Court in India, of an offence punishable under Chapter XII or Chapter XVII of this Code with imprisonment of either description for a term of three years or upwards, shall be guilty of any offence punishable under either of those Chapters with like imprisonment for the like term, shall be subject for every such subsequent offence to imprisonment for life, or to imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years.
ingredients: Previous conviction by a Court in India
For an offence under Chapter XII (coin and stamps) or Chapter XVII (property) punishable with imprisonment of 3 years or upwards
Subsequent offence under either Chapter punishable with like imprisonment for the like term

punishment_options.condition: Enhanced punishment for each subsequent offence

sections.key_principle: Habitual-offender enhancement for property and coin/stamp offences. Clause (b) (conviction by a court outside India) was omitted by Act 3 of 1951.
sections.amendment_note: Section substituted by Act 3 of 1910, s. 2; 'transportation for life' replaced by 'imprisonment for life' by Act 26 of 1955.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 3 of 1910, s. 2, for section 75.
The words 'British India' have successively been subs. by the A.O. 1948, the A.O. 1950 and Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch., to read as above.
The word 'or' omitted by Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch.
Cl. (b) omitted by s. 3 and the Sch., ibid.
Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

chapters.chapter_title: General Exceptions

chapters_covered: IV — General Exceptions
key_themes: Acts done under legal duty, mistake of fact or judicial authority (ss. 76–79)
Accident and necessity (ss. 80–81)
Infancy: under 7 absolute; 7–12 qualified (ss. 82–83)
Unsoundness of mind; involuntary vs voluntary intoxication (ss. 84–86)
Consent and benefit defences: ss. 87–89, 92, 93; limits on consent (ss. 90–91)
Duress — instant death threats, with murder and State offences excluded (s. 94)
De minimis harm (s. 95)
notable_amendments: Chapter IV applies to every offence by virtue of s. 6.
Section 94's exclusion of murder and capital offences against the State is a statutory limit on duress.
metadata.case_query: A surgeon operates without consent on an unconscious road-accident victim and the patient dies on the table; the family alleges culpable homicide. The surgeon claims he acted in good faith for the patient's benefit when consent was impossible.

sections.heading: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law
sections.text: Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law in good faith believes himself to be, bound by law to do it.
ingredients: Act done by a person who is bound by law to do it; OR
Who, by mistake of fact (not of law), in good faith believes himself bound by law to do it
sections.key_principle: Mistake of FACT, not law, protects a person who honestly believes he is legally bound to act. Ignorance of law is no excuse; good faith requires due care and attention (s. 52).

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A, a soldier, fires on a mob by the order of his superior officer, in conformity with the commands of the law. A has committed no offence.
illustrations.key_principle: Act done in obedience to a lawful order that the law commands is protected.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A, an officer of a Court of Justice, being ordered by that Court to arrest Y, and after due enquiry, believing Z to be Y, arrests Z. A has committed no offence.
illustrations.key_principle: A reasonable, good-faith mistake of fact (identity) after due enquiry is protected.

sections.heading: Act of Judge when acting judicially
sections.text: Nothing is an offence which is done by a Judge when acting judicially in the exercise of any power which is, or which in good faith he believes to be, given to him by law.
ingredients: Act done by a Judge
When acting judicially
In exercise of a power given by law, or which he in good faith believes to be given to him by law
sections.key_principle: Judicial immunity from criminal liability for judicial acts, extending to bona fide belief in power.

sections.heading: Act done pursuant to the judgment or order of Court
sections.text: Nothing which is done in pursuance of, or which is warranted by the judgment or order of, a Court of Justice; if done whilst such judgment or order remains in force, is an offence, notwithstanding the Court may have had no jurisdiction to pass such judgment or order, provided the person doing the act in good faith believes that the Court had such jurisdiction.
ingredients: Act done in pursuance of, or warranted by, a Court's judgment or order
Order remains in force at the time
Even if the Court lacked jurisdiction — provided the doer in good faith believes it had jurisdiction
sections.key_principle: Protects persons executing court orders (e.g. officers, bailiffs) even where the Court acted without jurisdiction, if they acted in good faith.

sections.heading: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself, justified, by law
