sections.text: Nothing is an offence which is done by any person who is justified by law, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law in good faith, believes himself to be justified by law, in doing it.
ingredients: Act done by a person justified by law; OR
Who by mistake of fact (not of law) in good faith believes himself justified by law
sections.key_principle: Companion to s. 76: s. 76 covers being 'bound' by law; s. 79 covers being 'justified' (permitted) by law. Mistake of fact only.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A sees Z commit what appears to A to be a murder. A, in the exercise, to the best of his judgment exerted in good faith, of the power which the law gives to all persons of apprehending murderers in the fact, seizes Z, in order to bring Z before the proper authorities. A has committed no offence, though it may turn out that Z was acting in self-defence.
illustrations.key_principle: Honest, careful but mistaken belief in a legal justification (citizen's arrest) is protected.

sections.heading: Accident in doing a lawful act
sections.text: Nothing is an offence which is done by accident or misfortune, and without any criminal intention or knowledge in the doing of a lawful act in a lawful manner by lawful means and with proper care and caution.
ingredients: Act done by accident or misfortune
Without any criminal intention or knowledge
In doing a lawful act
In a lawful manner, by lawful means
With proper care and caution
sections.key_principle: All elements must co-exist; want of proper care and caution destroys the exception (and may amount to negligence under s. 304A).

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A is at work with a hatchet; the head flies off and kills a man who is standing by. Here, if there was no want of proper caution on the part of A, his act is excusable and not an offence.
illustrations.key_principle: Genuine accident during a lawful act with due care is not an offence.

sections.heading: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm
sections.text: Nothing is an offence merely by reason of its being done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause harm, if it be done without any criminal intention to cause harm, and in good faith for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property.
ingredients: Act done with knowledge that it is likely to cause harm
Without criminal intention to cause harm
In good faith
For the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property
sections.key_principle: Doctrine of necessity / choice of lesser evil. Whether the harm avoided was so imminent and serious as to justify the risk is a question of fact.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A, the captain of a steam vessel, suddenly, and without any fault or negligence on his part, finds himself in such a position that, before he can stop his vessel, he must inevitably run down a boat B, with twenty or thirty passengers on board, unless he changes the course of his vessel, and that, by changing his course, he must incur risk of running down a boat C with only two passengers on board, which he may possibly clear. Here, if A alters his course without any intention to run down the boat C and in good faith for the purpose of avoiding the danger to the passengers in the boat B, he is not guilty of an offence, though he may run down the boat C by doing an act which he knew was likely to cause that effect, if it be found as a matter of fact that the danger which he intended to avoid was such as to excuse him in incurring the risk of running down C.
illustrations.verdict: No offence (if the danger justified the risk)
illustrations.key_principle: Choosing the lesser harm in good faith to avoid a greater, imminent harm is excused.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A, in a great fire, pulls down houses in order to prevent the conflagration from spreading. He does this with the intention in good faith of saving human life or property. Here, if it be found that the harm to be prevented was of such a nature and so imminent as to excuse A's act, A is not guilty of the offence.
illustrations.verdict: No offence (if harm was imminent enough)
illustrations.key_principle: Creating a firebreak by destroying property to save lives/property is justified by necessity.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: It is a question of fact in such a case whether the harm to be prevented or avoided was of such a nature and so imminent as to justify or excuse the risk of doing the act with the knowledge that it was likely to cause harm.
explanations.plain_language: The court decides on the facts whether the danger avoided was serious and imminent enough to justify the risk taken.

sections.heading: Act of a child under seven years of age
sections.text: Nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.
ingredients: Act done by a child
Under seven years of age
sections.key_principle: Absolute, irrebuttable presumption of incapacity (doli incapax) for children under seven. (Age raised for juveniles under the Juvenile Justice Act — separate regime.)

sections.heading: Act of a child above seven and under twelve of immature understanding
sections.text: Nothing is an offence which is done by a child above seven years of age and under twelve, who has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge of the nature and consequences of his conduct on that occasion.
ingredients: Child above seven and under twelve
Has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding
To judge the nature and consequences of his conduct on that occasion
sections.key_principle: Qualified immunity: rebuttable — the question is the child's actual maturity at the time of the act.

sections.heading: Act of a person of unsound mind
sections.text: Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law.
ingredients: Act done by a person of unsound mind
At the time of doing it
Incapable of knowing the nature of the act; OR
Incapable of knowing that it is wrong or contrary to law

mens_rea_modes.description: Incapacity to know the nature of the act
Incapacity to know the act is wrong or contrary to law

sections.key_principle: Insanity defence (M'Naghten-based). The test is the cognitive capacity at the time of the act; legal insanity, not medical insanity. The accused bears the burden of proof (Evidence Act s. 105) on a preponderance of probabilities.

sections.heading: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will
sections.text: Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, is, by reason of intoxication, incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong, or contrary to law; provided that the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will.
ingredients: Intoxication at the time of the act
Incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it is wrong/contrary to law
Intoxicant administered without his knowledge or against his will
sections.key_principle: Involuntary intoxication is a complete defence — voluntary intoxication is not (see s. 86).

sections.heading: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated
sections.text: In cases where an act done is not an offence unless done with a particular knowledge or intent, a person who does the act in a state of intoxication shall be liable to be dealt with as if he had the same knowledge as he would have had if he had not been intoxicated, unless the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will.
ingredients: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge
Act done in a state of intoxication
Deemed to have the knowledge he would have had if sober
Unless intoxicant was administered without his knowledge or against his will
sections.key_principle: Voluntary intoxication: knowledge is imputed, but intention must still be inferred from the facts — the court may consider whether the intoxicated person could form the specific intent (e.g. for murder).

sections.heading: Act not intended and not known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, done by consent
sections.text: Nothing which is not intended to cause death, or grievous hurt, and which is not known by the doer to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, to any person, above eighteen years of age, who has given consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm; or by reason of any harm which it may be known by the doer to be likely to cause to any such person who has consented to take the risk of that harm.
ingredients: Act not intended to cause death or grievous hurt
Not known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt
Harm to a person above eighteen years
Who has given consent (express or implied) to suffer that harm or take the risk
sections.key_principle: Consent defence for lesser harm: valid only for adults and only where neither death nor grievous hurt is intended or known to be likely (e.g. sports, fencing). Consent must be free of fear or misconception (s. 90).

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A and Z agree to fence with each other for amusement. This agreement implies the consent of each to suffer any harm which, in the course of such fencing, may be caused without foul play; and if A, while playing fairly, hurts Z, A commits no offence.
illustrations.key_principle: Participation in a sport implies consent to harm caused without foul play.

sections.heading: Act not intended to cause death, done by consent in good faith for person's benefit
sections.text: Nothing, which is not intended to cause death, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, or be known by the doer to be likely to cause, to any person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, and who has given a consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm, or to take the risk of that harm.
ingredients: Act not intended to cause death
Done in good faith for the benefit of the person
Person has given consent (express or implied) to suffer the harm or risk
sections.key_principle: Medical-treatment defence: even grievous hurt or risk of death (if death not intended) is excused where done with consent for the person's benefit. Unlike s. 87, no age limit stated here, but consent must be valid under s. 90.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, a surgeon, knowing that a particular operation is likely to cause the death of Z, who suffers under the painful complaint, but not intending to cause Z's death, and intending, in good faith, Z's benefit, performs that operation on Z, with Z's consent. A has committed no offence.
illustrations.key_principle: A surgeon acting in good faith, with consent, for the patient's benefit is protected even if death is likely.

sections.heading: Act done in good faith for benefit of child or insane person, by or by consent of guardian
sections.text: Nothing which is done in good faith for the benefit of a person under twelve years of age, or of unsound mind, by or by consent, either express or implied, of the guardian or other person having lawful charge of that person, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause or be known by the doer to be likely to cause to that person.
ingredients: Act done in good faith for the benefit of a person under twelve or of unsound mind
By, or with the consent (express/implied) of, the guardian or person in lawful charge
sections.key_principle: Guardian's substituted consent for children under 12 and persons of unsound mind. Four provisos limit it: no intentional killing; no likely-death acts except to save life/cure; no grievous hurt except to prevent death/grievous hurt or cure disease; no abetment beyond the exception.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, in good faith, for his child's benefit without his child's consent, has his child cut for the stone by a surgeon knowing it to be likely that the operation will cause the child's death, but not intending to cause the child's death. A is within the exception, inasmuch as his object was the cure of the child.
illustrations.key_principle: Operation for cure, with guardian's consent, falls within the exception even if death is likely (Proviso Secondly permits it for curing grievous disease).

provisos.text: This exception shall not extend to the intentional causing of death, or to the attempting to cause death.

This exception shall not extend to the doing of anything which the person doing it knows to be likely to cause death, for any purpose other than the preventing of death or grievous hurt, or the curing of any grievous disease or infirmity.

This exception shall not extend to the voluntary causing of grievous hurt, or to the attempting to cause grievous hurt, unless it be for the purpose of preventing death or grievous hurt, or the curing of any grievous disease or infirmity.
This exception shall not extend to the abetment of any offence, to the committing of which offence it would not extend.

sections.heading: Consent known to be given under fear or misconception
sections.text: A consent is not such a consent as is intended by any section of this Code, if the consent is given by a person under fear of injury, or under a misconception of fact, and if the person doing the act knows, or has reason to believe, that the consent was given in consequence of such fear or misconception; or if the consent is given by a person who, from unsoundness of mind, or intoxication, is unable to understand the nature and consequence of that to which he gives his consent; or, unless the contrary appears from the context, if the consent is given by a person who is under twelve years of age.
ingredients: Consent given under fear of injury, or misconception of fact, known (or reasonably believed) by the doer to be so caused; OR
Consent of a person of unsound mind or intoxicated, unable to understand nature and consequences; OR
Consent of a child under twelve (unless context shows otherwise)

clauses.heading: Consent known to be given under fear or misconception
clauses.text: Consent given by a person under fear of injury or under a misconception of fact, where the person doing the act knows or has reason to believe the consent was so caused.

clauses.heading: Consent of insane person
clauses.text: Consent given by a person who, from unsoundness of mind or intoxication, is unable to understand the nature and consequence of that to which he gives his consent.

clauses.heading: Consent of child
clauses.text: Unless the contrary appears from the context, consent given by a person who is under twelve years of age.

sections.key_principle: Negative definition of 'consent': vitiated by fear, misconception of fact, unsoundness of mind/intoxication, or tender age. Consent obtained by deception as to the nature of the act is no consent (e.g. rape provisions).

sections.heading: Exclusion of acts which are offences independently of harm caused
sections.text: The exceptions in sections 87, 88 and 89 do not extend to acts which are offences independently of any harm which they may cause, or be intended to cause, or be known to be likely to cause, to the person giving the consent, or on whose behalf the consent is given.
ingredients: Exceptions in ss. 87, 88 and 89 apply only to offences that depend on harm to the consenting person
They do not apply to acts that are offences independently of such harm
sections.key_principle: Consent defences cannot legalise acts that are offences in themselves (e.g. causing miscarriage, offences against public interest).

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: Causing miscarriage (unless caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the woman) is offence independently of any harm which it may cause or be intended to cause to the woman. Therefore, it is not an offence "by reason of such harm"; and the consent of the woman or of her guardian to the causing of such miscarriage does not justify the act.
illustrations.key_principle: Where the act is an offence regardless of harm to the person, consent does not justify it.

sections.heading: Act done in good faith for benefit of a person without consent
sections.text: Nothing is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause to a person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, even without that person's consent, if the circumstances are such that it is impossible for that person to signify consent, or if that person is incapable of giving consent, and has no guardian or other person in lawful charge of him from whom it is possible to obtain consent in time for the thing to be done with benefit.
ingredients: Act done in good faith for the person's benefit
Without consent because it is impossible for the person to signify consent, or the person is incapable of consenting
No guardian from whom consent can be obtained in time
sections.key_principle: Emergency (doctrine of necessity in medical practice): benefit without consent when consent is impossible and no guardian is available. Same four provisos as s. 89, with a stricter third proviso (hurt only to prevent death or hurt).

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: Z is thrown from his horse, and is insensible. A, a surgeon, finds that Z requires to be trepanned. A, not intending Z's death, but in good faith, for Z's benefit, performs the trepan before Z recovers his power of judging for himself. A has committed no offence.
illustrations.key_principle: Emergency surgery on an insensible patient without consent is protected.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: Z is carried off by a tiger. A fires at the tiger knowing it to be likely that the shot may kill Z, but not intending to kill Z, and in good faith intending Z's benefit. A's ball gives Z a mortal wound. A has committed no offence.
illustrations.key_principle: A risky rescue attempt in good faith for the person's benefit is protected.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A, a surgeon, sees a child suffer an accident which is likely to prove fatal unless an operation be immediately performed. There is not time to apply to the child's guardian. A performs the operation in spite of the entreaties of the child, intending, in good faith, the child's benefit. A has committed no offence.
illustrations.key_principle: Where there is no time to consult the guardian, emergency treatment of a child is protected.

illustrations.label: Illustration (d)
illustrations.text: A is in a house which is on fire, with Z, a child. People below hold out a blanket. A drops the child from the house top, knowing it to be likely that the fall may kill the child, but not intending to kill the child, and intending, in good faith, the child's benefit. Here, even if the child is killed by the fall, A has committed no offence.
illustrations.key_principle: A desperate rescue act with good-faith intent to benefit is excused even if death results.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: Mere pecuniary benefit is not benefit within the meaning of sections 88, 89 and 92.
explanations.plain_language: Financial gain alone cannot be the 'benefit' that justifies the act.

provisos.text: This exception shall not extend to the intentional causing of death, or the attempting to cause death.

This exception shall not extend to the doing of anything which the person doing it knows to be likely to cause death, for any purpose other than the preventing of death or grievous hurt, or the curing of any grievous disease or infirmity.
This exception shall not extend to the voluntary causing of hurt, or to the attempting to cause hurt, for any purpose other than the preventing of death or hurt.
This exception shall not extend to the abetment of any offence, to the committing of which offence it would not extend.

sections.heading: Communication made in good faith
sections.text: No communication made in good faith is an offence by reason of any harm to the person to whom it is made, if it is made for the benefit of that person.
ingredients: Communication made in good faith
For the benefit of the person to whom it is made
sections.key_principle: Protects honest communication of bad news (e.g. a medical prognosis) even if it causes harm such as shock.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, a surgeon, in good faith, communicates to a patient his opinion that he cannot live. The patient dies in consequence of the shock. A has committed no offence, though he knew it to be likely that the communication might cause the patient's death.
illustrations.key_principle: A good-faith communication for the patient's benefit is protected even if death results.

sections.heading: Act to which a person is compelled by threats
sections.text: Except murder, and offences against the State punishable with death, nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is compelled to do it by threats, which, at the time of doing it, reasonably cause the apprehension that instant death to that person will otherwise be the consequence: Provided the person doing the act did not of his own accord, or from a reasonable apprehension of harm to himself short of instant death, place himself in the situation by which he became subject to such constraint.
ingredients: Act compelled by threats
Threats reasonably cause apprehension of instant death to the doer
Not murder, nor an offence against the State punishable with death
Doer did not voluntarily place himself in the situation (or from fear of lesser harm)
sections.key_principle: Duress / compulsion defence: requires threat of INSTANT death; unavailable for murder and capital offences against the State; unavailable to those who voluntarily join criminal gangs.

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: A person who, of his own accord, or by reason of a threat of being beaten, joins a gang of dacoits, knowing their character, is not entitled to the benefit of this exception, on the ground of his having been compelled by his associates to do anything that is an offence by law.
explanations.plain_language: Voluntarily joining a criminal gang (even under threat of a beating) forfeits the duress defence.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: A person seized by a gang of dacoits, and forced, by threat of instant death, to do a thing which is an offence by law; for example, a smith compelled to take his tools and to force the door of a house for the dacoits to enter and plunder it, is entitled to the benefit of this exception.
explanations.plain_language: A person forcibly seized and compelled under threat of instant death may rely on the defence.

sections.heading: Act causing slight harm
sections.text: Nothing is an offence by reason that it causes, or that it is intended to cause, or that it is known to be likely to cause, any harm, if that harm is so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain of such harm.
ingredients: Act causes, intends, or is known likely to cause harm
Harm is so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain
sections.key_principle: De minimis non curat lex — trivial harms are not offences. Objective test of the person of ordinary sense and temper.

chapters.chapter_title: General Exceptions
chapters.sub_heading: Of the Right of Private Defence

chapters_covered: IV — General Exceptions (sub-heading: Of the Right of Private Defence)
key_themes: Private defence of body and property (ss. 96–97)
Defence against persons not criminally responsible (s. 98)
Limits: public servants, time to seek help, proportionality (s. 99)
When death may be caused in defence of the body (s. 100) and when only lesser harm (s. 101)
Commencement and continuance of the right of defence of the body (s. 102)
Defence of property: death only in four cases (s. 103); otherwise lesser harm (s. 104); duration (s. 105)
Deadly assault with risk to innocents (s. 106)
notable_amendments: Act 13 of 2013, s. 2 — clause 'Seventhly' (acid attack) added to s. 100 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).
Karnataka Act 8 of 1972 — amendment of s. 103 (mischief by explosive substance; places of worship; Government property).
metadata.case_query: A homeowner shoots and kills a burglar who has broken in at night and is running away with a TV; the homeowner argues private defence of property, while the prosecution says the burglar was no longer a threat.

sections.heading: Things done in private defence
sections.text: Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence.
ingredients: Act done in exercise of the right of private defence
sections.key_principle: Foundation of private defence: lawful exercise of the right is not an offence. Sections 97–106 define the scope, extent and duration of the right.

sections.heading: Right of private defence of the body and of property
sections.text: Every person has a right, subject to the restrictions contained in section 99, to defend— First.—His own body, and the body of any other person, against any offence affecting the human body; Secondly.—The property, whether movable or immovable, of himself or of any other person, against any act which is an offence falling under the definition of theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass, or which is an attempt to commit theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass.
ingredients: Right to defend one's own body or the body of any other person against any offence affecting the human body
Right to defend movable or immovable property (own or another's) against theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass, or attempts thereat
Subject to restrictions in s. 99
sections.key_principle: Right extends to defence of others (body and property). Property defence is limited to four offences: theft, robbery, mischief, criminal trespass (including attempts).

sections.heading: Right of private defence against the act of a person of unsound mind, etc.
sections.text: When an act, which would otherwise be a certain offence, is not that offence, by reason of the youth, the want of maturity of understanding, the unsoundness of mind or the intoxication of the person doing that act, or by reason of any misconception on the part of that person, every person has the same right of private defence against that act which he would have if the act were that offence.
ingredients: Act would be an offence but for the doer's youth, immaturity, unsoundness of mind, intoxication or misconception
Same right of private defence exists as if it were an offence
sections.key_principle: Private defence depends on the objective danger, not on the assailant's criminal responsibility.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: Z, under the influence of madness, attempts to kill A; Z is guilty of no offence. But A has the same right of private defence which he would have if Z were sane.
illustrations.verdict: A may defend himself as against a sane assailant
illustrations.key_principle: The assailant's insanity does not reduce the victim's right of private defence.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A enters by night a house which he is legally entitled to enter. Z, in good faith, taking A for a house-breaker, attacks A. Here Z, by attacking A under this misconception, commits no offence. But A has the same right of private defence against Z, which he would have if Z were not acting under that misconception.
illustrations.verdict: A has the right of private defence against Z
illustrations.key_principle: A mistaken (good-faith) attacker commits no offence, yet the target may defend himself.

sections.heading: Acts against which there is no right of private defence
sections.text: There is no right of private defence against an act which does not reasonably cause the apprehension of death or of grievous hurt, if done, or attempted to be done, by a public servant acting in good faith under colour of his office, though that act, may not be strictly justifiable by law. There is no right of private defence against an act which does not reasonably cause the apprehension of death or of grievous hurt, if done, or attempted to be done, by the direction of a public servant acting in good faith under colour of his office, though that direction may not be strictly justifiable by law. There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to protection of the public authorities. Extent to which the right may be exercised.—The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence.
ingredients: No right against public servants acting in good faith under colour of office (no reasonable apprehension of death/grievous hurt)
No right against acts done by direction of such a public servant
No right where there is time to have recourse to public authorities
Right never extends to inflicting more harm than necessary

clauses.text: No right of private defence against an act (not causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt) by a public servant acting in good faith under colour of his office.
No right against an act by the direction of such a public servant.
No right where there is time to have recourse to the protection of public authorities.
Extent: the right never extends to inflicting more harm than necessary for defence.

sections.key_principle: Four limits on private defence: (1) acts of public servants in good faith; (2) acts by their direction; (3) availability of time to seek police/state protection; (4) proportionality — no more harm than necessary. These limits are the basis of the 'excess of private defence' exception in s. 300 Exception 2.

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: A person is not deprived of the right of private defence against an act done, or attempted to be done, by a public servant, as such, unless he knows or has reason to believe, that the person doing the act is such public servant.
explanations.plain_language: The restriction applies only if the person knows or has reason to believe the actor is a public servant.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: A person is not deprived of the right of private defence against an act done, or attempted to be done, by the direction of a public servant, unless he knows, or has reason to believe, that the person doing the act is acting by such direction, or unless such person states the authority under which he acts, or if he has authority in writing, unless he produces such authority, if demanded.
explanations.plain_language: The restriction applies only if the person knows of the direction, or the actor states the authority or produces written authority on demand.

sections.heading: When the right of private defence of the body extends to causing death
sections.text: The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in the last preceding section, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the assailant, if the offence which occasions the exercise of the right be of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:— First.—Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; Secondly.—Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; Thirdly.—An assault with the intention of committing rape; Fourthly.—An assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; Fifthly.—An assault with the intention of kidnapping or abducting; Sixthly.—An assault with the intention of wrongfully confining a person, under circumstances which may reasonably cause him to apprehend that he will be unable to have recourse to the public authorities for his release; Seventhly.—An act of throwing or administering acid or an attempt to throw or administer acid which may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such act.
sections.inserted_by: Clause Seventhly inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 2 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013)
ingredients: Right of private defence of the body
Extends to voluntarily causing death or any other harm to the assailant
Only if the assault falls within one of the seven enumerated descriptions
Subject to the restrictions in s. 99

clauses.text: Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of such assault.
Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such assault.
An assault with the intention of committing rape.
An assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust.
An assault with the intention of kidnapping or abducting.

An assault with the intention of wrongfully confining a person, under circumstances which may reasonably cause him to apprehend that he will be unable to have recourse to the public authorities for his release.
An act of throwing or administering acid or an attempt to throw or administer acid which may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such act.

sections.key_principle: Death may be caused in defence of the body only against seven categories of assault. The test is REASONABLE APPREHENSION, judged objectively from the defender's position. Clause Seventhly (acid attacks) was inserted by Act 13 of 2013.

sections.heading: When such right extends to causing any harm other than death
sections.text: If the offence be not of any of the descriptions enumerated in the last preceding section, the right of private defence of the body does not extend to the voluntary causing of death to the assailant, but does extend, under the restrictions mentioned in section 99, to the voluntary causing to the assailant of any harm other than death.
ingredients: Offence not within the seven descriptions in s. 100
No right to cause death
Right extends to any harm other than death
Subject to s. 99 restrictions
sections.key_principle: Residual rule: for lesser assaults, force may be used but not to the extent of killing.

sections.heading: Commencement and continuance of the right of private defence of the body
sections.text: The right of private defence of the body commences as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body arises from an attempt or threat to commit the offence though the offence may not have been committed; and it continues as long as such apprehension of danger to the body continues.
ingredients: Commences on reasonable apprehension of danger from an attempt or threat
Offence need not have been committed
Continues as long as the apprehension continues
sections.key_principle: The right is preventive, not punitive: it arises on reasonable apprehension and ends when the danger ends. Retaliation after the threat has passed is not private defence.

sections.heading: When the right of private defence of property extends to causing death
sections.text: The right of private defence of property extends, under the restrictions mentioned in section 99, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the wrong-doer, if the offence, the committing of which, or the attempting to commit which, occasions the exercise of the right, be an offence of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:— First.—Robbery; Secondly.—House-breaking by night; Thirdly.—Mischief by fire committed on any building, tent or vessel, which building, tent or vessel is used as a human dwelling, or as a place for the custody of property; Fourthly.—Theft, mischief, or house-trespass, under such circumstances as may reasonably cause apprehension that death or grievous hurt will be the consequence, if such right of private defence is not exercised.
ingredients: Right of private defence of property
Extends to causing death or any other harm to the wrong-doer

Only against robbery; house-breaking by night; mischief by fire on dwelling/custody building, tent or vessel; theft, mischief or house-trespass causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt

clauses.text: Robbery.
House-breaking by night.
Mischief by fire committed on any building, tent or vessel, which building, tent or vessel is used as a human dwelling, or as a place for the custody of property.

Theft, mischief, or house-trespass, under such circumstances as may reasonably cause apprehension that death or grievous hurt will be the consequence, if such right of private defence is not exercised.

sections.key_principle: Defence of property can justify killing only in four graver situations; ordinary theft or trespass does not.

state_amendments.text: (1) In section 103, in clause Thirdly, (i) after the words 'mischief by fire', the words 'or any explosive substance' shall be inserted; (ii) after the words 'as a human dwelling, or' the words 'as a place of worship, or' shall be inserted. (2) After clause Fourthly, the following clause shall be inserted: 'Fifthly.—Mischief by fire or any explosive substance committed on any property used or intended to be used for the purpose of Government or any local authority, statutory body or company owned or controlled by Government or railway or any vehicle used or adapted to be used for the carriage of passengers for hire or reward.'

sections.heading: When such right extends to causing any harm other than death
sections.text: If the offence, the committing of which, or the attempting to commit which occasions the exercise of the right of private defence, be theft, mischief, or criminal trespass, not of any of the descriptions enumerated in the last preceding section, that right does not extend to the voluntary causing of death, but does extend, subject to the restrictions mentioned in section 99, to the voluntary causing to the wrong-doer of any harm other than death.
ingredients: Offence is theft, mischief or criminal trespass
Not of the s. 103 descriptions
No right to cause death
Right to cause any harm other than death, subject to s. 99
sections.key_principle: Residual rule for property defence — force short of death.

sections.heading: Commencement and continuance of the right of private defence of property
sections.text: The right of private defence of property commences when a reasonable apprehension of danger to the property commences. The right of private defence of property against theft continues till the offender has effected his retreat with the property or either the assistance of the public authorities is obtained, or the property has been recovered. The right of private defence of property against robbery continues as long as the offender causes or attempts to cause to any person death or hurt or wrongful restraint or as long as the fear of instant death or of instant hurt or of instant personal restraint continues. The right of private defence of property against criminal trespass or mischief continues as long as the offender continues in the commission of criminal trespass or mischief. The right of private defence of property against house-breaking by night continues as long as the house-trespass which has been begun by such house-breaking continues.
ingredients: Commences with reasonable apprehension of danger to property
Theft: till offender retreats with property, or public help obtained, or property recovered
Robbery: while offender causes/attempts death, hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death/hurt/restraint continues
Criminal trespass or mischief: while the offender continues the offence
House-breaking by night: while the house-trespass continues

clauses.text: Continues till the offender has effected his retreat with the property, or the assistance of the public authorities is obtained, or the property has been recovered.
Continues as long as the offender causes or attempts to cause to any person death or hurt or wrongful restraint, or as long as the fear of instant death, hurt or personal restraint continues.
Continues as long as the offender continues in the commission of criminal trespass or mischief.
Continues as long as the house-trespass which has been begun by such house-breaking continues.

sections.key_principle: Duration of the property-defence right is offence-specific; once the offence is over or help arrives, the right ends.

sections.heading: Right of private defence against deadly assault when there is risk of harm to innocent person
sections.text: If in the exercise of the right of private defence against an assault which reasonably causes the apprehension of death, the defender be so situated that he cannot effectually exercise that right without risk of harm to an innocent person, his right of private defence extends to the running of that risk.
ingredients: Assault reasonably causing apprehension of death
Defender cannot effectually defend without risk of harm to an innocent person
Right extends to running that risk
sections.key_principle: Necessity within private defence: the defender is not liable for harm to innocents that is an unavoidable risk of effectively repelling a deadly assault.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A is attacked by a mob who attempt to murder him. He cannot effectually exercise his right of private defence without firing on the mob, and he cannot fire without risk of harming young children who are mingled with the mob. A commits no offence if by so firing he harms any of the children.
illustrations.key_principle: Where defence against a deadly assault inevitably risks harm to innocents, the risk may be run.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Abetment

chapters_covered: V — Of Abetment
key_themes: Abetment defined — instigation, conspiracy, intentional aid (s. 107)
Who is an abettor; abetment complete without the offence; abetment of abetment (s. 108)
Abetment in India of offences abroad (s. 108A)
Punishment where act abetted is committed (s. 109); different intention (s. 110); different act (s. 111); cumulative (s. 112); different effect (s. 113); abettor present (s. 114)
Punishment where offence is not committed — death/life offences (s. 115), imprisonment offences (s. 116)
Abetment by the public / more than ten persons (s. 117)
Concealing design to commit offence — ss. 118–120
notable_amendments: Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 — 'transportation for life' replaced by 'imprisonment for life' in ss. 115, 118, 119.
Act 4 of 1898, s. 3 — s. 108A inserted.
Act 10 of 2009, s. 51 — encryption/information-hiding tools added to ss. 118 and 119; s. 118–120 added to the extended 'offence' list in s. 40.
metadata.case_query: A man gives a friend a gun, knowing the friend wants to shoot a rival, but the friend is arrested before he can carry out the plan; the man argues that since no offence was ever committed, he cannot be punished as an abettor.

sections.heading: Abetment of a thing
sections.text: A person abets the doing of a thing, who— First.—Instigates any person to do that thing; or Secondly.—Engages with one or more other person or persons in any conspiracy for the doing of that thing, if an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing; or Thirdly.—Intentionally aids, by any act or illegal omission, the doing of that thing.
ingredients: Instigation of any person to do the thing; OR
Engaging in a conspiracy to do the thing, with an act or illegal omission taking place in pursuance of the conspiracy; OR
Intentional aid, by act or illegal omission, to the doing of the thing

mens_rea_modes.description: Instigation — actively suggesting, stimulating or encouraging the act
Conspiracy — agreement plus an act or illegal omission in pursuance
Intentional aid — facilitating the act with intention

clauses.heading: Instigation
clauses.text: Instigates any person to do that thing.

clauses.heading: Conspiracy
clauses.text: Engages with one or more other person or persons in any conspiracy for the doing of that thing, if an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing.

clauses.heading: Intentional aid
clauses.text: Intentionally aids, by any act or illegal omission, the doing of that thing.

sections.key_principle: Three modes of abetment: instigation, conspiracy (plus an overt act/omission), intentional aid. Mere passive acquiescence or knowledge is not abetment; there must be positive instigation or intentional assistance.

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: A person who, by wilful misrepresentation, or by wilful concealment of a material fact which he is bound to disclose, voluntarily causes or procures, or attempts to cause or procure, a thing to be done, is said to instigate the doing of that thing.
explanations.plain_language: Instigation includes inducing someone to act by lying or by concealing a material fact one is bound to disclose.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, a public officer, is authorised by a warrant from a Court of Justice to apprehend Z. B, knowing that fact and also that C is not Z, wilfully represents to A that C is Z, and thereby intentionally causes A to apprehend C. Here B abets by instigation the apprehension of C.
illustrations.key_principle: Wilful misrepresentation that procures another's act is instigation.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: Whoever, either prior to or at the time of the commission of an act, does anything in order to facilitate the commission of that act, and thereby facilitates the commission thereof, is said to aid the doing of that act.
explanations.plain_language: Aid means actually facilitating the act, before or at the time it is done.

sections.heading: Abettor
sections.text: A person abets an offence, who abets either the commission of an offence, or the commission of an act which would be an offence, if committed by a person capable by law of committing an offence with the same intention or knowledge as that of the abettor.
ingredients: Abets the commission of an offence; OR
Abets the commission of an act which would be an offence if committed by a person capable by law of committing an offence with the same intention or knowledge as the abettor
sections.key_principle: An abettor is liable even where the principal is not criminally responsible (child, lunatic, person acting under mistake) and even if the abetted act is never committed. The abettor's own mens rea is what counts.

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: The abetment of the illegal omission of an act may amount to an offence although the abettor may not himself be bound to do that act.
explanations.plain_language: One can abet an illegal omission even when one is not under the duty to act.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: To constitute the offence of abetment it is not necessary that the act abetted should be committed, or that the effect requisite to constitute the offence should be caused.
explanations.plain_language: Abetment is complete on instigation/aid; the offence abetted need not occur.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A instigates B to murder C. B refuses to do so. A is guilty of abetting B to commit murder.
illustrations.key_principle: Instigation is punishable even if the person instigated refuses.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A instigates B to murder D. B in pursuance of the instigation stabs D. D recovers from the wound. A is guilty of instigating B to commit murder.
illustrations.verdict: A guilty of abetment of murder
illustrations.key_principle: The required effect (death) need not follow; the instigation is enough.

explanations.label: Explanation 3
explanations.text: It is not necessary that the person abetted should be capable by law of committing an offence, or that he should have the same guilty intention or knowledge as that of the abettor, or any guilty intention or knowledge.
explanations.plain_language: The person abetted need not be criminally responsible or share the abettor's guilty mind.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A, with a guilty intention, abets a child or a lunatic to commit an act which would be an offence, if committed by a person capable by law of committing an offence, and having the same intention as A. Here A, whether the act be committed or not, is guilty of abetting an offence.
illustrations.key_principle: Abetting an incapable person is still abetment.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A, with the intention of murdering Z, instigates B, a child under seven years of age, to do an act which causes Z's death. B, in consequence of the abetment, does the act in the absence of A and thereby causes Z's death. Here, though B was not capable by law of committing an offence, A is liable to be punished in the same manner as if B had been capable by law of committing an offence, and had committed murder, and he is therefore subject to the punishment of death.
illustrations.key_principle: The abettor of an incapable child is punished as if the child had committed the offence.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A instigates B to set fire to a dwelling-house. B, in consequence of the unsoundness of his mind, being incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is wrong or contrary to law, sets fire to the house in consequence of A's instigation. B has committed no offence, but A is guilty of abetting the offence of setting fire to a dwelling-house, and is liable to the punishment provided for that offence.
illustrations.verdict: A guilty of abetment; B no offence
illustrations.key_principle: An insane principal is not liable but the abettor is.

illustrations.label: Illustration (d)
illustrations.text: A, intending to cause a theft to be committed, instigates B to take property belonging to Z out of Z's possession. A induces B to believe that the property belongs to A. B takes the property out of Z's possession, in good faith, believing it to be A's property. B, acting under this misconception, does not take dishonestly, and therefore does not commit theft. But A is guilty of abetting theft, and is liable to the same punishment as if B had committed theft.
illustrations.verdict: A guilty of abetting theft; B no theft
illustrations.key_principle: Innocent agent: the abettor with the guilty intention is liable.

explanations.label: Explanation 4
explanations.text: The abetment of an offence being an offence, the abetment of such an abetment is also an offence.
explanations.plain_language: Abetment of abetment is itself an offence — liability runs up the chain.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A instigates B to instigate C to murder Z. B accordingly instigates C to murder Z, and C commits that offence in consequence of B's instigation. B is liable to be punished for his offence with the punishment for murder; and, as A instigated B to commit the offence, A is also liable to the same punishment.
illustrations.verdict: A and B both liable as for murder
illustrations.key_principle: Chain of instigation: each link is an abettor.

explanations.label: Explanation 5
explanations.text: It is not necessary to the commission of the offence of abetment by conspiracy that the abettor should concert the offence with the person who commits it. It is sufficient if he engages in the conspiracy in pursuance of which the offence is committed.
explanations.plain_language: A conspirator need not deal directly with the person who commits the offence; being part of the conspiracy suffices.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A concerts with B a plan for poisoning Z. It is agreed that A shall administer the poison. B then explains the plan to C mentioning that a third person is to administer the poison, but without mentioning A's name. C agrees to procure the poison, and procures and delivers it to B for the purpose of its being used in the manner explained. A administers the poison; Z dies in consequence. Here, though A and C have not conspired together, yet C has been engaged in the conspiracy in pursuance of which Z has been murdered. C has therefore committed the offence defined in this section and is liable to the punishment for murder.
illustrations.key_principle: Chain conspiracy: C is a conspirator though he never dealt with A.

sections.heading: Abetment in India of offences outside India
sections.text: A person abets an offence within the meaning of this Code who, in India, abets the commission of any act without and beyond India which would constitute an offence if committed in India.
ingredients: Abetment committed in India
Of an act outside India
Which would be an offence if committed in India
sections.key_principle: Extends abetment liability to abetment within India of foreign offences, closing the gap between ss. 3–4 (territorial reach) and abetment.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, in India, instigates B, a foreigner in Goa, to commit a murder in Goa, A is guilty of abetting murder.
illustrations.key_principle: Abetment within India of an offence is punishable here.

footnotes.note_text: Added by Act 4 of 1898, s. 3.
The words 'British India' have successively been subs. by the A.O. 1948, the A.O. 1950 and Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch., to read as above.

sections.heading: Punishment of abetment if the act abetted is committed in consequence and where no express provision is made for its punishment
sections.text: Whoever abets any offence shall, if the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made by this Code for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence.
ingredients: Abetment of an offence
The act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment
No express provision for punishing the abetment elsewhere in the Code

punishment_options.type: Same as the punishment for the abetted offence
punishment_options.condition: Where the act is committed in consequence of the abetment

sections.key_principle: General punishment clause for abetment: the abettor is punished as the principal where the offence follows from the abetment.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A offers a bribe to B, a public servant, as a reward for showing A some favour in the exercise of B's official functions. B accepts the bribe. A has abetted the offence defined in section 161.
illustrations.key_principle: The bribe-giver abets the public servant's offence of taking a gratification (s. 161 has since been repealed by the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988).

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A instigates B to give false evidence. B, in consequence of the instigation, commits that offence. A is guilty of abetting that offence, and is liable to the same punishment as B.
illustrations.key_principle: Abetment of an offence that is then committed attracts the same punishment.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A and B conspire to poison Z. A, in pursuance of the conspiracy, procures the poison and delivers it to B in order that he may administer it to Z. B, in pursuance of the conspiracy, administers the poison to Z in A's absence and thereby causes Z's death. Here B is guilty of murder. A is guilty of abetting that offence by conspiracy, and is liable to the punishment for murder.
illustrations.verdict: B guilty of murder; A guilty of abetment by conspiracy
illustrations.key_principle: Conspirators who supply the means are abettors punished as for the offence.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: An act or offence is said to be committed in consequence of abetment, when it is committed in consequence of the instigation, or in pursuance of the conspiracy, or with the aid which constitutes the abetment.
explanations.plain_language: 'In consequence' means the offence resulted from the instigation, conspiracy or aid.

sections.heading: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor
sections.text: Whoever abets the commission of an offence shall, if the person abetted does the act with a different intention or knowledge from that of the abettor, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence which would have been committed if the act had been done with the intention or knowledge of the abettor and with no other.
ingredients: Abetment of an offence
Person abetted acts with a different intention or knowledge
Abettor punished according to his own intention or knowledge

punishment_options.type: Punishment for the offence that would have resulted had the act been done with the abettor's own intention/knowledge
punishment_options.condition: Where the principal acts with a different mental state

sections.key_principle: The abettor is judged by his own mens rea — not the principal's (links to s. 108 Explanation 3 and s. 38).

sections.heading: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done
sections.text: When an Act is abetted and a different act is done, the abettor is liable for the act done, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had directly abetted it: Provided the act done was a probable consequence of the abetment, and was committed under the influence of the instigation, or with the aid or in pursuance of the conspiracy which constituted the abetment.
ingredients: One act abetted, a different act done
Act done was a probable consequence of the abetment
Committed under the influence of the instigation, or with the aid or in pursuance of the conspiracy
sections.key_principle: Probable-consequence rule: the abettor is liable for a different act actually done only if it was a probable consequence of the abetment and sprang from the abetment — not if it was a distinct, independent act.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A instigates a child to put poison into the food of Z, and gives him poison for that purpose. The child, in consequence of the instigation, by mistake puts the poison into the food of Y, which is by the side of that of Z. Here, if the child was acting under the influence of A's instigation, and the act done was under the circumstances a probable consequence of the abetment, A is liable in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had instigated the child to put the poison into the food of Y.
illustrations.verdict: A liable as if he had instigated poisoning Y
illustrations.key_principle: A mistaken execution that is a probable consequence remains attributable to the abettor.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A instigates B to burn Z's house. B sets fire to the house and at the same time commits theft of property there. A, though guilty of abetting the burning of the house, is not guilty of abetting the theft; for the theft was a distinct act, and not a probable consequence of the burning.
illustrations.verdict: A guilty of abetting arson, not theft
illustrations.key_principle: A distinct act that is not a probable consequence is outside the abetment.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A instigates B and C to break into an inhabited house at midnight for the purpose of robbery, and provides them with arms for that purpose. B and C break into the house, and being resisted by Z, one of the inmates, murder Z. Here, if that murder was the probable consequence of the abetment, A is liable to the punishment provided for murder.
illustrations.verdict: A liable for murder if probable consequence
illustrations.key_principle: Providing arms for a night break-in makes a fatal resistance a probable consequence.

sections.heading: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done
sections.text: If the act for which the abettor is liable under the last preceding section is committed in addition to the act abetted, and constitute a distinct offence, the abettor is liable to punishment for each of the offences.
ingredients: Act done under s. 111 is committed in addition to the act abetted
It constitutes a distinct offence
Abettor liable to punishment for each offence

punishment_options.condition: For both the act abetted and the distinct act done

sections.key_principle: Cumulative liability where the extra act is a probable consequence of the abetment (an exception to the no-double-punishment idea in s. 71).

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A instigates B to resist by force a distress made by a public servant. B, in consequence, resists that distress. In offering the resistance, B voluntarily causes grievous hurt to the officer executing the distress. As B has committed both the offence of resisting the distress, and the offence of voluntarily causing grievous hurt, B is liable to punishment for both these offences; and, if A knew that B was likely voluntarily to cause grievous hurt in resisting the distress A will also be liable to punishment for each of the offences.
illustrations.verdict: B liable for both; A liable for both if he knew grievous hurt was likely
illustrations.key_principle: Abettor's knowledge that the additional offence was likely makes him liable for both.

sections.heading: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by the act abetted different from that intended by the abettor
sections.text: When an act is abetted with the intention on the part of the abettor of causing a particular effect, and an act for which the abettor is liable in consequence of the abetment, causes a different effect from that intended by the abettor, the abettor is liable for the effect caused, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had abetted the act with the intention of causing that effect, provided he knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect.
ingredients: Act abetted with intention of causing a particular effect
Act causes a different effect
Abettor knew the act abetted was likely to cause that effect
Liable as if he had abetted with the intention of causing that effect
sections.key_principle: Different result: the abettor is liable for the actual effect only if he knew it was likely.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A instigates B to cause grievous hurt to Z. B, in consequence of the instigation, causes grievous hurt to Z. Z dies in consequence. Here, if A knew that the grievous hurt abetted was likely to cause death, A is liable to be punished with the punishment provided for murder.
illustrations.verdict: A liable for murder if he knew death was likely
illustrations.key_principle: Knowledge that the abetted hurt was likely to cause death makes the abettor liable for the resulting death.

sections.heading: Abettor present when offence is committed
sections.text: Whenever any person, who is absent would be liable to be punished as an abettor, is present when the act or offence for which he would be punishable in consequence of the abetment is committed, he shall be deemed to have committed such act or offence.
ingredients: Person who, if absent, would be liable as an abettor
Present when the act or offence is committed
Deemed to have committed the act or offence

punishment_options.condition: Abettor present at the commission is treated as having committed the offence

sections.key_principle: Constructive presence: an abettor present at the scene is treated as a principal.

sections.heading: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life — if offence not committed
sections.text: Whoever abets the commission of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, shall, if that offence be not committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made by this Code for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine; if act causing harm be done in consequence.—and if any act for which the abettor is liable in consequence of the abetment, and which causes hurt to any person, is done, the abettor shall be liable to imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to fourteen years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Abetment of an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment
Offence not committed in consequence of the abetment
No express punishment provision elsewhere
(Second limb) Act causing hurt done in consequence

punishment_options.condition: Up to seven years and also fine — offence not committed
Up to fourteen years and also fine — if an act causing hurt is done in consequence of the abetment

sections.key_principle: Abetment of capital/life offences that is unsuccessful: 7 years; 14 years if hurt results.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A instigates B to murder Z. The offence is not committed. If B had murdered Z, he would have been subject to the punishment of death or imprisonment for life. Therefore A is liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and also to a fine; and if any hurt be done to Z in consequence of the abetment, he will be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to fourteen years, and to fine.
illustrations.verdict: A: up to 7 years + fine; up to 14 years + fine if hurt results
illustrations.key_principle: Unsuccessful instigation to murder carries 7 years; if hurt follows, 14 years.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment — if offence be not committed
sections.text: Whoever abets an offence punishable with imprisonment shall, if that offence be not committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made by this Code for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term provided for that offence; or with such fine as is provided for that offence, or with both; if abettor or person abetted be a public servant whose duty it is to prevent offence.—and if the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant, whose duty it is to prevent the commission of such offence, the abettor shall be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the longest term provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both.
ingredients: Abetment of an offence punishable with imprisonment
Offence not committed in consequence
No express provision elsewhere
(Aggravated) abettor or person abetted is a public servant whose duty is to prevent the offence

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment of any description provided for the offence
punishment_options.condition: Up to one-fourth of the longest term

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment of any description provided for the offence
punishment_options.condition: Up to one-half of the longest term — if abettor or abetted is a public servant whose duty is to prevent the offence

sections.key_principle: Unsuccessful abetment of imprisonment offences: one-fourth of the maximum; one-half if the abettor or the abetted is a public servant bound to prevent the offence.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A offers a bribe to B, a public servant, as a reward for showing A some favour in the exercise of B's official functions. B refuses to accept the bribe. A is punishable under this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Attempted bribery is abetment of an offence that was not committed.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A instigates B to give false evidence. Here, if B does not give false evidence, A has nevertheless committed the offence defined in this section, and is punishable accordingly.
illustrations.key_principle: Instigation is complete even if the false evidence is never given.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A, a police-officer, whose duty it is to prevent robbery, abets the commission of robbery. Here, though the robbery be not committed, A is liable to one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for that offence, and also to fine.
illustrations.verdict: A liable to up to one-half of the longest term, and fine
illustrations.key_principle: Public servant bound to prevent the offence faces the aggravated punishment.

illustrations.label: Illustration (d)
illustrations.text: B abets the commission of a robbery by A, a police-officer, whose duty it is to prevent that offence. Here, though the robbery be not committed, B is liable to one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for the offence of robbery, and also to fine.
illustrations.verdict: B liable to up to one-half of the longest term, and fine
illustrations.key_principle: The enhancement applies where the person abetted is such a public servant.

sections.heading: Abetting commission of offence by the public or by more than ten persons
sections.text: Whoever abets the commission of an offence by the public generally or by any number or class of persons exceeding ten, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Abetting the commission of an offence
By the public generally, or by any number or class of persons exceeding ten
sections.key_principle: Mass abetment — instigation addressed to the public at large or more than ten persons. The offence is complete without the offence being committed.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A affixes in a public place a placard instigating a sect consisting of more than ten members to meet at a certain time and place, for the purpose of attacking the members of an adverse sect, while engaged in a procession. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
illustrations.key_principle: A public placard inciting more than ten persons to attack is abetment by the public.

sections.heading: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life
sections.text: Whoever intending to facilitate or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby facilitate the commission of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, voluntarily conceals by any act or illegal omission, or by the use of encryption or any other information hiding tool, the existence of a design to commit such offence or makes any representation which he knows to be false respecting such design, shall, if that offence be committed, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or, if the offence be not committed, with imprisonment of either description, for a term which may extend to three years; and in either case shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Intending to facilitate, or knowing it likely that he will facilitate, an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment
Voluntarily conceals the existence of a design (by act, illegal omission, encryption or information hiding tool); OR
Makes a representation known to be false respecting the design

punishment_options.condition: Up to seven years and fine — if the offence is committed
Up to three years and fine — if the offence is not committed

sections.key_principle: Concealment of a design to commit a capital/life offence. The 2009 amendment extends concealment to encryption and information hiding tools.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, knowing that dacoity is about to be committed at B, falsely informs the Magistrate that a dacoity is about to be committed at C, a place in an opposite direction, and thereby misleads the Magistrate with intent to facilitate the commission of the offence. The dacoity is committed at B in pursuance of the design. A is punishable under this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Misleading the authorities about a planned dacoity facilitates it and is punishable.

sections.amendment_note: The words 'voluntarily conceals by any act or illegal omission, or by the use of encryption or any other information hiding tool, the existence of a design' were substituted by Act 10 of 2009, s. 51 (w.e.f. 27-10-2009).

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 10 of 2009, s. 51, for 'voluntarily conceals, by any act or illegal omission, the existence of a design' (w.e.f. 27-10-2009).

sections.heading: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent
sections.text: Whoever, being a public servant intending to facilitate or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby facilitate the commission of an offence which it is his duty as such public servant to prevent, voluntarily conceals, by any act or illegal omission or by the use of encryption or any other information hiding tool, the existence of a design to commit such offence, or makes any representation which he knows to be false respecting such design, shall, if the offence be committed, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the longest term of such imprisonment, or with such fine as is provided for that offence, or with both; or, if the offence be punishable with death or imprisonment for life, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years; or, if the offence be not committed, shall be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term of such imprisonment or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both.
ingredients: Offender is a public servant
Offence is one which it is his duty to prevent
Conceals the design (act, illegal omission, encryption or information hiding tool) or makes a false representation about it
Intending to facilitate, or knowing it likely to facilitate, the offence

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment of any description provided for the offence
punishment_options.condition: Up to one-half of the longest term, or fine, or both — if the offence is committed
Up to ten years — if the offence is punishable with death or life imprisonment

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment of any description provided for the offence
punishment_options.condition: Up to one-fourth of the longest term, or fine, or both — if the offence is not committed

sections.key_principle: Aggravated concealment by a public servant bound to prevent the offence — higher punishments than s. 118/120.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, an officer of police, being legally bound to give information of all designs to commit robbery which may come to his knowledge, and knowing that B designs to commit robbery, omits to give such information, with intent to facilitate the commission of that offence. Here A has by an illegal omission concealed the existence of B's design, and is liable to punishment according to the provision of this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Failure by a police officer to disclose a known robbery plan, intending to facilitate it, is punishable.

footnotes.note_text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment
sections.text: Whoever, intending to facilitate or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby facilitate the commission of an offence punishable with imprisonment, voluntarily conceals, by any act or illegal omission, the existence of a design to commit such offence, or makes any representation which he knows to be false respecting such design, shall, if the offence be committed, be punished with imprisonment of the description provided for the offence, for a term which may extend to one-fourth, and, if the offence be not committed, to one-eight, of the longest term of such imprisonment, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both.
ingredients: Intending to facilitate, or knowing it likely that he will facilitate, an offence punishable with imprisonment
Voluntarily conceals the existence of the design, or makes a representation known to be false

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment of the description provided for the offence
punishment_options.condition: Up to one-fourth of the longest term — if the offence is committed

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment of the description provided for the offence
punishment_options.condition: Up to one-eighth of the longest term — if the offence is not committed

sections.key_principle: Concealment of a design to commit a lesser (imprisonment-only) offence — fractional punishment: 1/4 if committed, 1/8 if not.

chapters.chapter_title: Criminal Conspiracy

chapters_covered: VA — Criminal Conspiracy
key_themes: Definition of criminal conspiracy — agreement to do an illegal act or a legal act by illegal means (s. 120A)
Overt act requirement for non-offence conspiracies (proviso to s. 120A)
Punishment of criminal conspiracy: same as abetment for serious offences; up to six months for others (s. 120B)
notable_amendments: Chapter VA inserted by Act 8 of 1913, s. 3.
metadata.case_query: Three friends agree to illegally download copyrighted films for resale, but never do anything beyond the agreement; they argue that no conspiracy exists without any overt act.

sections.heading: Definition of criminal conspiracy
sections.text: When two or more persons agree to do, or cause to be done,— (1) an illegal act, or (2) an act which is not illegal by illegal means, such an agreement is designated a criminal conspiracy: Provided that no agreement except an agreement to commit an offence shall amount to a criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties to such agreement in pursuance thereof.
ingredients: Agreement between two or more persons
To do or cause to be done an illegal act; OR an act which is not illegal by illegal means
(Where the agreed object is not an offence) some overt act besides the agreement in pursuance of it
sections.key_principle: The gist is the agreement itself. Where the agreement is to commit an offence, no overt act is needed; where the object is merely illegal (not an offence), or a legal act by illegal means, an overt act is required.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: It is immaterial whether the illegal act is the ultimate object of such agreement, or is merely incidental to that object.
explanations.plain_language: The illegal act may be only a means to the ultimate object; the conspiracy still exists.

footnotes.note_text: Ins. by Act 8 of 1913, s. 3 (Chapter VA).

sections.heading: Punishment of criminal conspiracy
sections.text: (1) Whoever is a party to a criminal conspiracy to commit an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment for a term of two years or upwards, shall, where no express provision is made in this Code for the punishment of such a conspiracy, be punished in the same manner as if he had abetted such offence.
